questions.question_text: Match List–I with List–II and select the correct answer using the code given below: List–I List–II A. 1854 AD 1. Sir Charles Wood's Despatch on Education B. 1882 AD 2. Sadler University Commission C. 1904 AD 3. Hunter Education Commission D. 1917 AD 4. Indian University Act
questions.explanation: List-I List-II 1854 AD – Sir Charles Wood's Despatch on education 1882 AD – Hunter Commission (related to education) 1904 AD – Indian University Act 1917 AD – Sadler University Commission

questions.question_text: Who was the first Indian Vice-Chancellor of Calcutta University among the following?
questions.explanation: Asutosh Mukherjee is chosen as the creator of modern Bengal. Mukherjee was the first Indian who traveled across entire India as a member of the Royal Commission (Sadler Commission). Curzon wanted to stop higher education through the Indian University Act. Mukherjee, with the help of the same Act, raised Calcutta University from being an examination-taking institution to a higher postgraduate education institution. Later, Mukherjee also became its Vice-Chancellor

questions.question_text: In which legislation was the word ‘Scheduled Castes’ used for the first time?
questions.explanation: In the Government of India Act of 1935, the word 'Scheduled Caste' was used for the first time. There was such a provision in the Act in which Dr. B.R. Ambedkar considered the provision of separate electorate as the only hope for Dalits to get political representation

questions.question_text: Who among the following was not a famous Orientalist?
questions.explanation: Charles Trevelyan was a British officer and he did administrative work. He worked in the colonies of Calcutta from 1850 to 1860. He worked in modern India, not in the Orientalist while H. T. Colebrooke, H. H. Wilson, Edwin Arnold, James Prinsep, and Alexander Cunningham are all three Orientalists

questions.question_text: Which of the following Acts increased the proportion of female voters and gave them reserved seats in the Legislative Assembly?
questions.explanation: UGC NET-II Paper Nov. 2017 Explanation– The Government of India Act, 1935 was the result of national movements from 1920 to 1935. This bill was passed on 2 August 1935. This Act, without a preamble, was the largest and most complex document in the history of the British Parliament, in which there were 14 parts, 10 appendices, 321 sections, and 10 schedules. By the Act of 1935, a federal government was established in India for the first time. By the Act of 1935, the proportion of female voters was increased and they were given reserved seats in the Legislative Assembly.

questions.question_text: Who was the first Chancellor of the first Indian Women's University among the following?
questions.explanation: UGC NET-II Paper Nov. 2017 Explanation– The first Chancellor of the first Indian Women's University was Sir R.G. Bhandarkar. Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar (6 July, 1837-24 August, 1925) was a scholar, oriental historian, and social reformer of India. He was the first modern indigenous historian of India. Bhandarkar was not against the British, but he was wealthy in nationalist consciousness. He was the first such indigenous historian who opposed the foreign-influenced theories on Indian civilization strongly and logically.

questions.question_text: What is the name of the Act under which the printer and publisher of any indigenous language newspaper had to give a pledge not to publish material inciting feelings of discontent against the government?
questions.explanation: UGC NET-III Paper Nov. 2017 Explanation– That Act is the Vernacular Press Act, 1878 which was passed during the time of Lord Lytton. Under which the printer and publisher of any indigenous language newspaper had to give a pledge not to publish material inciting feelings of discontent against the government.

questions.question_text: In which year was the Birth Control League established in Bombay?
questions.explanation: UGC NET-III Paper Nov. 2017 Explanation– Birth Control League was established in Bombay in 1924.

questions.question_text: Which two of the following four universities were established in the same year? Choose the correct answer from the code given below–
questions.explanation: UGC NET-III Paper Nov. 2017 UGC Net.- III Paper June. 2015 Explanation– Among the mentioned universities, S.N.D.T. Women's University and Banaras Hindu University were established in the same year, i.e., 1916 A.D. Whereas Aligarh Muslim University was established in 1920 A.D. and Visva-Bharati University was established in 1921 A.D.

questions.question_text: Which of the following acts was described by Jawaharlal Nehru as the 'New Charter of Slavery'?
questions.explanation: UGC NET-II Paper Jan. 2017 Explanation– Jawaharlal Nehru described the Government of India Act, 1935 as the 'New Charter of Slavery'. Through this, a plan was made to establish a federation for India, in which the provinces of British India and those princely states that wished to join voluntarily were to be included.

questions.question_text: Who was the first professor appointed at Elphinstone Institute, Bombay in 1835?
questions.explanation: – Bal Gangadhar Jambhekar (1812-1846) was appointed as the first professor of India in 1835 at Elphinstone Institute, Bombay, in mathematics as an assistant to Prof. Orlebar

questions.question_text: When was the first school for women established in Rawalpindi?
questions.explanation: – The first school for women in Rawalpindi was established in December 1856

questions.question_text: In which year was Tarabai Shinde's famous book 'Stri-Purush Tulana' published?
questions.explanation: – Tarabai Shinde's (1850-1910) famous book ''Stri Purush Tulana'' was published in 1882

questions.question_text: The Vernacular Press Act IX of 1878 was passed on 14 March and was implemented in all provinces except Madras because

options.A: The local residents of Madras were British supporters.
options.B: Only English newspapers were being published from Madras at that time.
options.C: The press of Indian languages had not yet become strong there.
options.D: Most of the vernacular printing presses in Madras were owned by the British.

questions.explanation: The Vernacular Press Act IX of 1878: Lord Lytton passed it on 14 March. It was passed due to the famine of 1876-78 and the criticism happening over the Delhi Durbar of 1877. It was implemented on all provinces except Madras because the press of Indian languages had not yet become strong in Madras. There were 19 vernacular newspapers in Madras

questions.question_text: Who among the following was the editor of the 'Bombay Chronicle', who was deported?
questions.explanation: In 1913, Ferozeshah Mehta founded the 'Bombay Chronicle' under the editorship of B.G. Horniman. Its main objective was to convey its message to the public after the Surat split of the Congress. Due to anti-government policies, B.G. Horniman was deported

questions.question_text: By which constitutional reform was the beginning of Dyarchy at the provincial level made?
questions.explanation: Government of India Act 1919 or Montague-Chelmsford Reform – British India Secretary Edwin Montagu and Viceroy Lord Chelmsford laid the foundation of these reforms. In this, the size of the provincial legislative councils was increased. Under this bill, the system of Dyarchy was implemented in the provinces. Provincial subjects were divided into two parts – Reserved and Transferred subjects. Reserved subjects were administered by the Governor with the help of his executive councillors, and Transferred subjects were administered by elected members

questions.question_text: By which of the following acts was a separate electorate proposed for Muslims in India?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Council Act (Morley-Minto) reform of 1909 (1) Separate electorate proposed for Muslims in India (2) Provided representation to Indians in both law-making and administration (3) Through this, along with the budget, the right to ask supplementary questions was received, although the right to vote was not yet received, but they could demand funds for local bodies.

questions.question_text: Under the 1935 Act, in the 1937 elections, the Congress achieved a massive majority and formed ministries in many provinces. Which of the following provinces was not one of them?
questions.explanation: In the provincial legislative elections held in January-February 1937, the Congress achieved a complete majority in five out of 11 provinces. It formed its governments in Madras, United Provinces, Central Provinces, Bihar, Odisha, Bombay (almost). Later, the Congress also formed cabinets in the North-West Frontier Province and Assam; only in Bengal, Punjab, and Sindh was the Congress deprived of a majority

questions.question_text: Two statements are given below, one is called Assertion (A) and the other is called Reason (R) – Assertion (A) : The British started Western education in India. Reason (R) : They wanted to make Indians aware of scientific and national progress. In the context of the above statements, which of the following is correct? Code :

options.C: (A) is true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.D: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- II Paper Dec. 2012) Explanation– Western education was started in India by Munro and Elphinstone, which Macaulay supported. Macaulay wanted to create such a group for the propagation of Western education among Indians, who would be Indian in color and blood, but English in thoughts, taste, and intellect. Macaulay believed that a shelf of a good European library is more valuable than all the literature of India and Arabia. The British certainly started Western education in India, but it was not the intention that they wanted to make Indians aware of national progress; rather, their purpose was only to get cooperation in administrative tasks so that British interests could be strengthened. Contrary to this, the commission has considered both statements true.

questions.question_text: Arrange the following commissions in chronological order and select the correct answer from the codes given below : (i) Kothari Commission (ii) Radhakrishnan Commission (iii) Sadler Commission (iv) University Grants Commission Code :
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper Dec. 2013) Explanation– Correct Answer– (i) Sadler Commission (1917) (ii) Radhakrishnan Commission (1948-49) (iii) University Grants Commission (1956) (iv) Kothari Commission (1964-66)

questions.question_text: Which of the following policy documents is called the 'Magna Carta' of Western education system in India?
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper Dec. 2013) Explanation– In the year 1854, Charles Wood prepared a document for changes in the Indian education system and sent it to the then Governor General Lord Dalhousie. Charles Wood's document of 1854 is called the 'Magna Carta' of the Western education system in India.

questions.question_text: Two statements are being given below, one is called Assertion (A) and the other is called Reason (R) – Assertion (A) : Macaulay's Law Commission, which was formed in 1860, destroyed the idea of India's land of 'Oriental Despotism'. Reason (R) : Equality and justice began to be seen as an alternative to the 'blind and harsh' justice of despotic rulers. Read the above statements and select the correct answer from the given code – Code :

options.C: Both (A) and (R) are correct, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.D: Both (A) and (R) are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- II Paper Dec. 2013) Explanation– After the Charter of 1833, Lord Macaulay was appointed as the Law Member of the Governor General's Executive Council. His contribution remained in the codification of law. He also had an important role in starting Western education in India.

questions.question_text: Which act was given the name 'Gagging Act'?
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper June. 2014) Explanation– The credit for passing the Vernacular Press Act 1878 goes to Lord Lytton. Under this, the government tried to bring Indian language newspapers under more control and made it a more successful weapon to suppress and punish seditious writings. It is also called the Gagging Act. Later in 1882 A.D., Ripon abolished this act.

questions.question_text: The act that ended the trade monopoly of the East India Company with India was:
questions.explanation: UGC Net.- III Paper June. 2014 PGT History, 2003 TGT History, 2010 Explanation– East India Company Act 1813 is also known as Charter Act 1813. Under this act, the trade monopoly of the East India Company with India was ended, only tea and trade rights with China remained.

questions.question_text: Which of the following was not a part of the Government of India Act, 1935?
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper Dec. 2014) Explanation– Through the Government of India Act 1935, provisions were made to implement Dyarchy at the central level and to establish partial responsible government. In this act, a provision was made for the establishment of a new central Reserve Bank, which was kept out of the control of the assembly. There was also a provision for a central court. The most prominent feature of this act was the establishment of provincial autonomy.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the regulations issued by Lord Wellesley for the control of the press in India?

options.A: Owners and editors of newspapers were asked to mention their name on their publication,
options.B: They were asked to publish news regarding the then ongoing war in Europe.
options.C: On any kind of violation of the regulations, they were immediately sent back to Europe.
options.D: Censorship was imposed on all newspapers under the regulations.

questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper June. 2015) Explanation– Lord Wellesley first of all, in 1799 A.D., passed a Press Control Act to establish control over the Indian press, which is as follows– (1) The newspaper editor, printer, and owner had to clearly print their names. (2) The publisher had to send all elements to be published to the government secretary for pre-censorship. (3) Imposed censorship on all newspapers. (4) English editors creating trouble for the administration were sent back to London. In 1818 A.D., Lord Hastings ended pre-censorship.

questions.question_text: During the rule of the British East India Company, who first established systematic press regulations?
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- II Paper June. 2015) Explanation– First of all, Lord Wellesley imposed censorship on all newspapers and in 1799 A.D., passed the Press Censorship Act. According to this, the newspaper editor, printer, and owner had to clearly print their names. The publisher had to send all elements to be published to the government secretary for pre-censorship.

questions.question_text: Where were High Courts established between 1886 and 1919?
questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- II Paper June. 2015) Explanation– Between 1886 and 1919 A.D., Allahabad, Patna and Lahore High Courts were established. The Patna High Court was established in 1916 A.D. Its circuit bench was Ranchi. The circuit bench of Allahabad High Court is Lucknow.

questions.question_text: Which of the following critical arguments regarding Dyarchy (Daikarchy) is not logical?

options.A: Defective division of subjects at the provincial level
options.C: Lack of finance for transferred subjects
options.D: Newly appointed ministers were inexperienced and incompetent.

questions.explanation: (UGC Net.- III Paper Dec. 2015) Explanation– Dyarchy was implemented through the Government of India Act 1919. Under this act, a system of Dyarchy was arranged in the provinces, under which provincial subjects were divided into transferred and reserved subjects. In the given option, the statement about ministers being inexperienced is wrong. The remaining options are correct.

questions.question_text: By which of the following acts was the Governor General of India empowered to issue ordinances?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2013 Explanation – This law of 1861 A.D. was an important step in the constitutional development of India. From this law, that policy of the British started which was named 'policy of cooperation' or 'liberal despotism' because through this, for the first time, an attempt was made to involve Indians in governance and the Governor General was given the power to issue ordinances when needed, which could remain in force for up to six months if not terminated by the Legislative Council or the Secretary of State for India.

questions.question_text: Who was not a member of the Governor General's Council established by the 'Regulating Act' of 1773?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2010 Explanation– In the Governor General's council established by the 'Regulating Act' of 1773, councillors Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson, and Barwell were members. Under this act, an administrative board was made in Bengal, in which the Governor General (as chairman) and four councillors were appointed. In this board, decisions were taken by majority and the chairman could only use a casting vote in the situation of equal votes. Philip Francis and Warren Hastings's mutual disagreement continued for a long time. Therefore, the above four options are correct.

questions.question_text: D.A.V. College was first established in–
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2005 Explanation– The biggest influence of the Arya Samaj's work area was seen in the field of education and social reform service. After Dayanand's death, there was a disagreement in the Arya Samaj regarding the medium of education. In 1886, Dayanand Anglo Vedic (D.A.V.) College was established in Lahore. It was founded by Lala Hansraj.

questions.question_text: The foundation year of the 'Constituent Assembly' is–
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2005 Explanation– Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, in the first elections of the Constituent Assembly held in July 1946, the Congress got 208, Muslim League 73, and other parties got 15 seats. The meeting of the Constituent Assembly started on 9 December 1946 under the chairmanship of Sachchidananda Sinha (Temporary President). On 11 December 1946, Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President. On 31 December 1946, Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar was elected chairman of the drafting committee of the constitution and B.N. Rau was its secretary.

questions.question_text: Through which act was the first constitutional interference made by the British Parliament in Indian affairs?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2004 (Cancelled) Explanation – The first constitutional interference by the British Parliament in Indian affairs was made through the Regulating Act of 1773. According to this Act, the burden of governance in India rested on the Governor General and his four-member council. Although the chairman of this council would be the Governor General, as far as the question of decision is concerned, they were based on majority. The casting vote of the Governor General was for the majority. Its members Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson, Barwell, and Governor General Warren Hastings were as members.

questions.question_text: Which English newspaper did Bal Gangadhar Tilak edit?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2004 (Cancelled) Explanation– Bal Gangadhar Tilak edited an English newspaper named 'Maratha' for the propagation of his thoughts. He also edited a newspaper in Marathi named 'Kesari' on 2 January 1881. Tilak created a wave of self-rule in the general public through his newspaper.

questions.question_text: Who among the following were the first to bring a printing press to India?
questions.explanation: The Portuguese were the first to bring a printing press to India. The first Portuguese traveler Vasco da Gama reached the coast of Calicut in India in 1498 A.D. After him, the Dutch were the ones to come to India. After this, the British came to India for trade

questions.question_text: When was provincial autonomy granted–
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2000 Explanation – In 1935 AD, provincial autonomy was granted in India. It is noteworthy that among the constitutional proposals, the Government of India Act 1935 was the last one. Its most prominent feature was – the establishment of provincial autonomy. Under this, the end of dual government in the provinces and the establishment of full responsible government took place.

options.A: There was a provision for separate representation and electoral college for Muslims.
options.B: Women did not have the right to be voters, but they could be candidates.
options.C: The majority of government members was maintained in this.
options.D: The members of the legislative council received the right to ask supplementary questions

questions.explanation: PGT History, 2000 Explanation – Through the Government of India Act 1909, separate voting rights and separate electoral districts were established for Muslims. This same change was made by the 1909 Act. About this act, K.M. Munshi wrote that ''They have killed the emerging democracy.''
examinations: Which change was made by the Government of India Act of 1909–

questions.question_text: Who established Visva-Bharati University?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2002 Explanation– Visva-Bharati University was established in 1921 A.D. by Rabindranath Tagore. This university is in Kolkata (West Bengal).

questions.question_text: Where was the 'Supreme Court' first established by the Regulating Act?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2004 Explanation– By the 1773 Regulating Act, a Supreme Court was established in Calcutta. It is noteworthy that by the Government of India Act 1935, a Federal Court was established.

questions.question_text: Who started the publication of the 'The Bengalee' newspaper?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2004 Explanation– The Bengalee newspaper was published by Surendranath Banerjee in 1879 A.D. This newspaper was published in the English language from Calcutta.

questions.question_text: Who gave permission for women's education in India?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2004 Explanation – Governor General Lord Dalhousie gave permission for women's education in India. It is noteworthy that Charles Wood's Dispatch came in 1854 A.D. during Dalhousie's time.

questions.question_text: Who was appointed the first Law Specialist?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2004 PGT History, 2011 Explanation– By the Charter Act 1833, a provision was made for the appointment of a Law Specialist in the Governor General's executive council. Lord Macaulay was appointed the first Law Specialist. It is noteworthy that by this same act, the Governor General of Bengal was made the Governor General of India.

questions.question_text: In 1784, the 'Asiatic Society of Bengal' was established in Calcutta?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2005, 2009, 2010, 2013 Explanation– In 1783, William Jones arrived in India. He had a special attachment to Indian culture. For the realization of ancient Indian glory, the Asiatic Society of Bengal was established by him in Calcutta in 1784.

questions.question_text: Which of the following universities was not established in 1857?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2009 Explanation – On the basis of Charles Wood's declaration letter, to expand Indian education, on the model of London University, three universities (Calcutta, Bombay and Madras) were established in India in 1857 A.D., whereas Allahabad University was made a university in 1887 by converting Muir Central College. These universities were management-based. Their job was only to look at administrative work. Academic work used to happen in affiliated colleges.

questions.question_text: Who first started English education in India?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2010 Explanation– Lord Macaulay is considered the father of English, i.e., Western education in India. On 2 February 1835, through his memorandum, Macaulay laid the foundation of English education in India while sharply criticizing Indian language and literature.

questions.question_text: Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College was established in
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2010 TGT History, 2005 Explanation – The current Aligarh Muslim University was established in 1875 by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan under the name Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College.

questions.question_text: By whom was the Constituent Assembly established?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2010 Explanation – On 24 March 1946, the 'Cabinet Mission' came to India. Members of this mission included Sir Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander, and Pethick Lawrence (Chairman). The establishment of India's Constituent Assembly was one of the main objectives of this mission.

questions.question_text: By which act was the Public Service Commission first established in India?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2010 Explanation – The Public Service Commission was first established in India in 1926 A.D. by the Government of India Act, 1919. By the 1935 Act, there was a provision for the formation of a Public Service Commission in the states in addition to the Union.

questions.question_text: The British government took the first step towards the expansion of modern education–
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation – Charter Act: In 1813, for the first time, a provision was made to spend 1 lakh rupees for the encouragement of Western education and literature.

questions.question_text: The act which reduced the number of directors of the court from 24 to 18 was–
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation – By the Charter Act of 1853, this arrangement was made that the Control Board and its other officers' salaries would be ensured by the government, but the money would be given by the company. The number of directors was reduced from 24 to 18, in which 6 were to be nominated by the Crown.

questions.question_text: Who among the following were supporters of freedom of the press?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation – Charles Metcalfe, Lord Hastings, and Lord Macaulay, all three were supporters of freedom of the press. In which Charles Metcalfe is called the 'Liberator' of newspapers.

questions.question_text: By whom was the Famine Commission appointed?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation – In 1878, a Famine Commission was established under the chairmanship of Richard Strachey to investigate the severe famine (1876-1878) in the Deccan by Viceroy Lord Lytton (1876-1880).

questions.question_text: Who were the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court established by the Government of India Act, 1935?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation– By the Government of India Act 1935, a Federal Court was established, in which there was a provision for the appointment of a Chief Justice and 6 other judges. Their appointment was done by the Emperor. This court became functional from 1 October 1937. It had original, appellate, and advisory jurisdiction. Its first Chief Justice was ‘Sir Maurice M. Gwyer’. Among the other 6 judges, two were Indians. First ‘Justice M.R. Jayakar’ and second Justice Shah Muhammad Sulaiman.

questions.question_text: The act which Jawaharlal Nehru called the Charter of Slavery –
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2011 Explanation – Jawaharlal Nehru called the Government of India Act, 1935, the Charter of Slavery and a car without an engine with many brakes.

questions.question_text: By whom was the proposal to establish an education department in every federal region of India made?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2013 Explanation – By the 1854 A.D. Charles Wood Dispatch, a proposal was made to establish an education department in every federal region of India. It is called the Magna Carta of Indian education.

questions.question_text: According to the Regulating Act, which of the following was not a member of the Council of the Governor General of Bengal?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2009 Explanation- The Regulating Act 1773 was passed. According to this, the burden of governance in India was put on the Governor General and his 4-member council. In this, decisions were taken by majority. Warren Hastings and Barwell were in India, and Clavering, Francis, and Monson were in England in October 1774. In 1777 A.D., Clavering died.

questions.question_text: Who founded the 'Primary Education Association'?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2009 Explanation- Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on 2 October 1869 in Porbandar, Gujarat. In 1893, he went to South Africa to fight a merchant's case, where he lived for 22 years and returned to India in 1915 and participated in the Indian freedom movement. He wanted such an education system, so that people could earn their livelihood in cottage industries. He founded the "Primary Education Association".

questions.question_text: In which of the following acts was a provision made for the post of Governor General of Bengal for the first time?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2009 Explanation- The British government passed the Regulating Act of 1773 A.D. to remove the corruption and maladministration prevalent in the company. Under this, the Madras and Bombay presidencies were placed under the Calcutta Bengal Presidency. Its head was a Governor General. The control of the Governor General was absolute.

questions.question_text: Which parliamentary act granted the Governor General of Bengal supervisory authority over Madras and Bombay?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2009 G.I.C. Lect. Exam 2009 Explanation- The rule of the company in India started from Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha. The Governor of Bengal was made the Governor-General of all three presidencies (Bengal, Bombay, and Madras) and Madras and Bombay were placed under Bengal. Through this same act, a Supreme Court was established in Calcutta. For the help of the Governor General, four members were appointed.

questions.question_text: In which area did the fundamental change come in the British policy in India in the 1813 Charter Act?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2009 Explanation- By the 1813 order letter, recognition was given to the British Parliament and King over the company's rule in India. For the first time, the company thought about the education of Indians, under which a provision was made to spend one lakh rupees every year for the education of Indians from the company's income. Under this act, Christian missionaries were given permission for Christian religious propagation in India.

questions.question_text: In which year was the English medium implemented in the education system in India?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2012 UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2009 Explanation– By the Charter of 1813, for the first time, the company government took the limited responsibility of Indian education. Consequently, the amount spent on education items was fixed at 1 lakh rupees every year. But there was a dispute over what should be the medium of education, which is also called the famous Anglicist-Orientalist dispute. Finally, after Macaulay's efforts, the English language was given priority and Macaulay's memorandum (Minute) gave recognition to English in 1835.

questions.question_text: Which section during the British period was against religious and social discrimination?
questions.explanation: G.I.C. Lect. Exam 2012 Explanation- During the British period, Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 was against religious and social discrimination. The then British government wanted more and more educated Indians to support us, for this it took various measures.

questions.question_text: According to which act was Burma separated from India?
questions.explanation: G.I.C. Lect. Exam 2015 Explanation- Under the Government of India Act 1935, Burma was separated from India. Dyarchy was ended in the provinces and Dyarchy was implemented at the centre. A Federal Court was established in India. Two new provinces, Sindh and Odisha, were formed.

questions.question_text: For the first time, a 'separate electorate' system was arranged.

options.C: Under Minto-Morley Reform 1909 (Indian Council Act of 1909)

questions.explanation: Higher Edu. Exam. (Med. History) 2013 UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2005 Explanation- The worst aspect of the Morley-Minto reforms of 1909 A.D. was providing the facility of separate or communal electoral system to Muslims. Over time, this facility poisoned the communal public life of India and ultimately acted as the sowing of seeds for the partition of the country.

questions.question_text: Under which act did the British East India Company give up its commercial activities?
questions.explanation: Higher Edu. Exam. (Med. History) 2014 Explanation– The Charter Act of 1833 gave a new life to the company for the next 20 years and established it as an entity. The commercial rights of the company were ended and it was to do only political work in the future. Through this act, the centralization of Indian administration was done. The Governor of Bengal was made the Governor General of India. The Governor General-in-Council was entrusted with the control, supervision, and direction of the military and civil works of the company.

questions.question_text: Which of the following provisions was not in Pitt's India Act?

options.A: A Board of Control was established in London which had six members
options.B: The number of members of the Governor General's council was reduced from four to three
options.C: The Board of Control was to manage the political, administrative, and commercial activities of the company
options.D: The Board of Directors was to manage only the commercial activities of the company

questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2002 Explanation- To remove the flaws of the Regulating Act, Britain's Prime Minister Pitt made this act in 1784 A.D. The sections of this act were as follows: An authority council for the governance of the company in India was established. Britain's King had the right to appoint and remove its members. The Finance Minister and Foreign Minister of Britain were its members. A secret council of the company's directors was made, which sent most orders to India. The number of members of the Governor General's council of India was reduced from four to three. Madras and Bombay were placed under the Governor General. In 1786, some other laws were also made, according to one of which the Governor General was given the right to work against the opinion of his council from time to time and he was also appointed the commander-in-chief of the British army in India.

questions.question_text: In which year was the Vernacular Press Act passed?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2002 UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2008, 2010 Explanation- During the time of British Governor General Lord Lytton, the Indian Language Newspaper Act was made in 1878. According to the Ninth Act of 1878, which had a provision for better control over publications in Eastern languages, the magistrate could issue orders to the publisher of any Indian language newspaper. It could write a bond from them for writing articles spreading dissatisfaction towards the government among the public and hatred among people of different castes and religions. The government also had the right that in the crime of publishing undesirable subjects, it could warn the related paper or take security from it, confiscate the security, and if that crime was repeated, the government could also confiscate the press. S.N. Banerjee called it the 'slaughter in the sky'.

questions.question_text: Which newspaper expressed the idea that ''The development of railways in India is a shackle''?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2004 Explanation- Under the Vernacular Press Act (Native Language Newspaper Act) passed by Lytton in 1878 A.D., which is also called the Gagging Act, cases were filed against newspapers like Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, Sahachar, etc. The 'Sahachar' newspaper mentioned the development of railways in India as a shackle.

questions.question_text: The proponents of the filtration theory in India's education policy were-
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2004, 2008 UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2010, 2011 Explanation- Macaulay is considered the main architect of the filtration theory (Downward Filtration Theory) in India's education policy. Bentinck appointed his legal member Macaulay as the chairman of the education committee. On 2 February 1835 A.D., Macaulay presented his thoughts in a special document. He termed Indian education and knowledge as very low. Supported the Western education system and supported making English the medium of education. In 1836 A.D., on the basis of his report, English was accepted as the medium of education and Western education as the basis of India's education system. Macaulay believed that the government could arrange education for Indians in some quantity with its limited resources and those educated Indians could look after the education of other Indians or the education and knowledge of Indian languages.

questions.question_text: With the implementation of education through English medium, help was received in India-

options.A: In making the British the supreme political power in India
options.B: In making Indians capable of getting high posts in the government
options.C: In the development and promotion of All-India Nationalism
options.D: In separating Indians from their ancient culture

questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2004 Explanation- With the implementation of education through English medium, help was received in increasing the development and promotion of All-India nationalism. The origin of national consciousness, birth of nationalism, and the start of national movement are generally credited to the Western modern education system. Raja Ram Mohan Roy was a supporter of English education. Supporting the importance of scientific education, he said 'If it is the government's policy that the country should be kept in darkness, then Sanskrit education system will be of greater benefit'. The government gave strength to the expansion of both English and Oriental languages. Therefore, in 1817, a grant was given for the building of Calcutta Hindu College, where education was given through English medium and Western science and technology were taught. Macaulay said about the use, importance, and claim of the English language that 'whoever knows this language has easy access to that great intellectual knowledge which the wisest creatures of the world have produced and has been transferred for the last 40 generations'.

questions.question_text: Which of the following acts declared the Sati system illegal?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2005 Explanation– In December 1829, Lord William Bentinck declared burning widows illegal under Regulation 17 and considered those who encouraged it as offenders of manslaughter. In 1830 A.D., this law was implemented in Madras and Bombay.

questions.question_text: Which act wrote the obituary on the grave of the East India Company?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2006 Explanation : The Act of 1858 wrote the obituary on the grave of the East India Company. According to this act, the rule of India was to be run by a Chief Secretary, who was now termed as Secretary of State for India, on behalf of the British Empress and a 15-member council was made for his help. This Secretary of State now received the powers used by both the Board of Directors and the Board of Control. Thus, the double government system implemented by the Pitt's India Act of 1784 was ended. It is noteworthy that this act came into existence during the tenure of British Prime Minister Lord Derby, whereas during the revolt of 1857, the British Prime Minister was Lord Palmerston.

questions.question_text: The first Englishman to acquire knowledge of Sanskrit was :
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2006 Explanation : The first Englishman to acquire knowledge of Sanskrit was Charles Wilkins. Wilkins translated 'Gita' and 'Hitopadesha' and also invented the letters for Persian and Bengali printing. The preface of Wilkins' first translation of the Gita was written by Lord Warren Hastings. Sir William Jones established the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784 in Calcutta, so that the social and natural history, archaeology, art, science, and literary study of Asia could be done. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's inscriptions in 1837 A.D. and revealed their secrets. Max Muller : (1823-1900) was a famous German scholar, he brought out a pure version of the Rigveda and translated it into English.

questions.question_text: After the end of the East India Company's rule, independent High Courts were established in 1861- 1. In Allahabad 2. In Bombay 3. In Calcutta Select the correct answer from the code below : Code : 4. In Madras
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2007 Explanation- As a result of the exploitative policy of the British Empire, several revolts took place after the establishment of the company. However, the most important and effective revolt among these was the great revolution of 1857. The consequences of this revolution brought many important changes in the policies of the British government. First of all, the ruling power was snatched from the company and given to the British Crown. Now, instead of Governor General, the Viceroy started running the governance as a representative of the British Crown. Among these changes, one important change was the establishment of independent High Courts in 1861 A.D. These High Courts were - Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras. The Allahabad High Court was established in 1868 A.D.

questions.question_text: Which was the first Urdu newspaper?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2007 Explanation- Some historians consider the Urdu newspaper named 'Jam-i-Jahan-Numa' published from Calcutta in 1822 A.D. by Harihar Datta as the first Urdu newspaper, but the first Urdu newspaper was 'Fauji-e-Akbar' or the military newspaper published by Tipu Sultan. Which started as a monthly newspaper in 1794 A.D.

questions.question_text: Who said, "Bentinck filled the Eastern despotism with the spirit of British freedom"?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2008, 2010 Explanation– William Bentinck was appointed the successor of Lord Amherst in 1828. Bentinck was a staunch liberal and was inspired by the same ideals from which the era of reforms in England started. In the laudatory words of Lord Macaulay – which were carved on his statue in Calcutta – 'Bentinck filled the Eastern despotism with the spirit of British freedom.'

questions.question_text: Sadler Commission is associated with?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2008 Explanation– In 1917, the government appointed a commission to study the possibilities of Calcutta University and for report. Dr. M.E. Sadler, who was the Vice-Chancellor of Leeds University, was appointed its Chairman. Dr. Sir Asutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin Ahmed were its Indian members.

questions.question_text: The 1833 Charter Act had some provisions. Select the correct answer on the basis of the code given below: (i) It ended the company's trade monopoly. (ii) It included a Law Member in the Governor General's council. (iii) It took back the law-making right of the presidencies. (iv) It changed the name of the Governor General of Fort William to Governor General of India. Code :

options.D: All of the above are true

questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2008 Explanation - By the 1833 Charter Act, the company's commercial rights were ended and it had to do only political work in the future. The Governor of Bengal was made the Governor General of India, and the Governor-General-in-Council was entrusted with the control, supervision, and direction of the military and civil works of the company. Through this act, a legal member was included in the Governor General's council for making laws, as a fourth member. By this act, the power of law-making was also centralized and now only the Governor General-in-Council was given the right to make laws for India, and the law-making power of the legislative assemblies of Bombay and Madras was ended.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is J.E.D. Bethune deeply associated with?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2008 Explanation - The actual work of women's education in India was done by J.E.D. Bethune, who was the Chairman of the Education Council. He established a girls' school in Calcutta in 1849.

questions.question_text: In which year was the 'Pitt's India Act' passed?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2005 Explanation– Pitt's India Act was passed by the British Parliament in 1784. Under this, the commercial and political activities of the company were separated from each other. All military, civil, and revenue-related matters of the company were placed under the 'Board of Control'. The number of members of the Governor General's council of India was reduced from four to three.

questions.question_text: 'Bengal Gazette' newspaper was –
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2010 Explanation – 'The Bengal Gazette' published in 1780 by James Augustus Hicky is considered the first newspaper of India. This newspaper of Augustus Hicky was weekly. The first attempt in the field of independent and neutral journalism in India was made by Hicky and Buckingham through the publication of the 'Calcutta Journal'.

questions.question_text: By which of the following acts was the 'Control Board' arranged?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2011 Explanation – Through Pitt's India Act 1784, two major changes came into the company's constitution. First, a department of the government was formed in England, which was called the Board of Control, and whose main task was to control the policy of the directors, and in this way, a dual system of governance, one by the company and the other by the parliamentary board, was created, and this continued until 1858.

questions.question_text: Hunter Commission placed special emphasis on the development of:

Its control should be handed over to district and municipal boards. An education cess could also be imposed on this. The Hunter Commission also gave its suggestions on secondary education

questions.question_text: Which regiment started the rebellion of 1857 in Berhampore?
questions.explanation: The rebellion of 1857 AD started due to the widespread religious sentiments hurt among the soldiers. After the spread of the news about the use of cartridges greased with cow and pig fat in the 'New Enfield Rifle', the 19th Native Infantry deployed in Berhampore rebelled, but the British successfully suppressed this rebellion right there. Subsequently, on 29 March 1857, the 34th Native Infantry rebelled in Barrackpore cantonment under the leadership of Mangal Pandey, and Mangal Pandey killed the military officer Adjutant. Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857

questions.question_text: In connection with the participation of Dalits in the rebellion of 1857, which of the following statements is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: The rebellion of 1857 is considered one of the important events of history. This rebellion first happened on 29 March 1857 in Barrackpore cantonment regarding the refusal by soldier Mangal Pandey and his companions to use grease-filled cartridges. Because soldiers in the British army came especially from Bengal, Awadh, and North-Western provinces. Most of them were Brahmins and Rajputs and they were not ready to accept the army's discipline. Many heroes led the war in different regions in 1857. In this, the leadership of northern Chotanagpur of Jharkhand was led by Thakur Vishwanath Shahdeo. As a result of which they were hanged in 1858 The name of Jhalkaribai is prominent in ensuring the participation of Dalits in 1857. She was born in a Koli family of Bhojla village (Jhansi). She was the commander of the women's branch 'Durga Dal' in the army of Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi. Prof. Badri Narayan Tiwari has done extensive research on the oral history of Dalit narratives of 1857. In 2004, his English book 'Multiple Marginalities: An Anthology of Identified Dalit Writings' was published. 4. Two statements are given below: one as an Assertion (A) and the other as its Reason (R): Assertion (A): In its Act XIV of June 1857, the Governor General's Supreme Council in Calcutta gave special commissions extraordinary power to catch and punish the rebels of 1857. Reason (R): The 'Causes of the Indian Revolt' (1858) in which the then sub-judge Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's primary objective was to show the loyalty of Muslims, who were viewed with suspicion and dislike in the years after the rebellion. In the light of the above statements, select the most appropriate answer from the options given below: (a) (A) and (R) both are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A). (b) (A) and (R) both are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (c) (A) is true, but (R) is not true. (d) (A) is not true, but (R) is true. (b) (A) and (R) both are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). (c) (A) is true, but (R) is not true. (d) (A) is not true, but (R) is true. NTA UGC NET/JRF Dec 2020/June 2021 Shift-I Ans. (b): In the first war of independence, the revolution of 1857, Lord Canning made many rules and military laws to crush the rebellion, in which the Supreme Council of the Governor General in Calcutta through Act XIV in June 1857 gave special commissions extraordinary power to catch and punish the rebels of 1857 and in this, the military officers got judicial powers. Not only was martial law imposed across North India, but military officers and common British people were also given the right to prosecute and punish rebels. Reason (R): Causes of the Indian Revolt (1858) - Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817-1898) was in judicial service in the company at the time of the 1857 rebellion, and remained completely loyal to the company, which led to the government's perception in 1857 that Muslims were responsible for this conspiracy. Sir Syed Ahmed asked for the support and service of the British to modernize the perspective of Muslims. He tried to end the Peer-Muridi system, slavery system. And propagated his ideas through 'Tehzeeb-ul-Akhlaq' (Civilization and Morality). Through 'Commentary on the Quran', he criticized traditional commentators. In 1875, he started the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental School in Aligarh, which later became Aligarh University in 1920. Note - Assertion (A) and Reason (R) both are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.question_text: Mangal Pandey was related to which rebellion?
questions.explanation: Mangal Pandey, with his companions of the 34th Regiment in Barrackpore (near Murshidabad), rebelled on 29 March 1857 by killing Adjutant Lieutenant Baugh and shooting Major Sergeant Hewson. The immediate cause of this rebellion was the use of the New Enfield Rifle instead of the old iron-made Brown Bess gun. In this rifle, the upper part of the cartridge had to be bitten by mouth, which contained cow and pig fat. This incident acted as a spark and Mangal Pandey rebelled

questions.question_text: Which of the following British military officers was responsible for the killing of Bahadur Shah's two sons?
questions.explanation: The rebels of Meerut reached Delhi on 11 May and on 12 May 1857 AD, they captured Delhi and declared Bahadur Shah II as the Emperor of India. A council was formed in Delhi to run government affairs and to settle all military and non-military matters. Initially, it was being led by the Mughal princes. But on 3 July 1857 AD, when Bakht Khan came from Bareilly, he was made the chief leader. On 20 September 1857, the British captured Delhi, but Nicholson was killed in this struggle. Hodson shot and killed the emperor's two sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and grandson Mirza Abu Bakr in front of the Red Fort of Delhi and arrested Bahadur Shah II from near Humayun's tomb.

questions.question_text: Mangal Pandey was a soldier of which regiment?
questions.explanation: The immediate cause of the 1857 rebellion was the use of the New Enfield Rifle instead of the old iron-made Brown Bess gun by the government in 1856 AD. In this rifle, the upper part of the cartridge had to be bitten by mouth. In January 1857 AD, a rumor spread in the Bengal army that the cartridge contained cow and pig fat. On 29 March 1857 AD, Mangal Pandey of the 34th Regiment Barrackpore (near Murshidabad) rebelled with his companions and killed Adjutant Lieutenant Baugh and shot Major Sergeant Hewson. Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April

questions.question_text: Who was leading the revolution of 1857 in Lucknow?
questions.explanation: There was dissatisfaction among the people due to the removal of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh from the throne on the basis of maladministration. Leaders like Maulvi Ahmadullah of Faizabad tried to take advantage of this situation. They instigated people for Jihad. In this context, Nana Saheb and Azimullah Khan came to Lucknow. On 30 May 1857 AD, the soldiers of Lucknow rebelled. On 14 June, Begum Hazrat Mahal took command of the rebellion and declared her minor son Birjis Qadir as the Nawab

questions.question_text: Who said in 1857 that "The desire to rule over Hindustan is not in me"?
questions.explanation: On 21 September, 1857 AD, Delhi was recaptured by the British, but John Nicholson was killed in this struggle. Hodson shot and killed the emperor's two sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and grandson Mirza Abu Bakr in front of the Red Fort of Delhi. questions.question_text: In which year was the Governor General of India also given the title of Viceroy?
questions.explanation: After the great revolution of 1857, the governance and administration of India were given a new direction and after ending the Company's rule, the reins of direct rule of India were given to Britain, for which the Government of India Act of 1858 was passed, whose main features are as follows– 1- The rule of East India Company was ended and handed over to the British Crown. The Governor General now began to be called Viceroy. 2- All rights of the Board of Directors and Board of Control were handed over to the Secretary of State for India. The Secretary of State for India was a member of the British Cabinet, for whose assistance a 15-member Indian Council was formed. Out of this, 7 members were appointed by the Court of Directors and 8 members by the British Government. Their expenses were borne by the Indian revenue. 3- Except for emergent works from the Indian revenue, for military operations carried out outside the boundaries of India.

questions.question_text: Who was the first Indian woman socialist and the first Indian woman revolutionary who fought for the freedom of her motherland after the rebellion of 1857?
questions.explanation: Famous revolutionary brave woman Bhikaiji Cama of India's freedom struggle was born on 24 September, 1861 AD in Mumbai. She went to London for treatment in 1902 AD, where she met Dadabhai Naoroji and her interest in the freedom struggle gradually increased. Started publishing a newspaper named Vande Mataram and kept campaigning among the public against British atrocities. In the socialist conference of the world organized in 1907 AD, Bhikaiji represented the people of India. And there, seeing the flags of other nations, Bhikaiji also made India's national flag and hoisted it. It had three stripes of red, yellow, and green colors. A lotus flower was on the green stripe and these flowers represented the eight provinces of India. 'Vande Mataram' was written in Devanagari script on the yellow stripe and sun and moon were made on the red stripe below

questions.question_text: When was the Clemency Resolution passed?
questions.explanation: Clemency Resolution, which is also called 'Clemency', which was brought through a proposal of 31 July 1857 AD, which distinguished between soldiers of those regiments who had rebelled and killed their officers and European citizens

questions.question_text: In which battle among the following did Tantia Tope defeat Raja Prithvi Singh of Jhalawar?
questions.explanation: Tantia Tope came to Rajasthan twice during the revolution of 1857. The second time, the king of Jhalawar, Prithvi Singh, was a friend of the British, who sent his army to capture Tantia Tope. But his platoon refused to fight and Tantia Tope captured Jhalawar. After this, a treaty was made between the two and Prithvi Singh provided Tantia Tope with five lakh rupees, military aid, weapons, and then made his state independent. After Jhalawar, Tantia Tope captured Baswara and received help in the revolution of 1857 from Rajasthan.

questions.question_text: Who wrote the book 'The Great Rebellion'?
questions.explanation: The book 'The Great Rebellion' is written on the great rebellion of 1857. Its author is Shri Ashok Mehta. Historians have expressed different opinions about the nature of the rebellion of 1857. Some called it a military rebellion, some called it a religious rebellion, etc. British historians have attempted to popularize these ideas that this was a war between barbarism and civilization. In this context, Ashok Mehta has also addressed it by calling it a national rebellion

questions.question_text: What was the main reason for the General Service List Act (1856), the rebellion of 1857?

options.A: It required soldiers to go abroad for deployment, which was forbidden for Hindus in those days.
options.B: It reduced the salary of soldiers.
options.C: It increased recruitment from high caste Hindus like Brahmins and Rajputs.
options.D: It promoted racism among the ranks of soldiers.

questions.explanation: In 1856 AD, Lord Canning's government passed the 'General Service Enlistment Act', according to which all future soldiers of Bengal had to accept that wherever the government needed them, they would work there. The British, reminding of the troubles of the first Anglo-Afghan war, were unwilling to send an army force by land to Herat. In India, the government attempted to start a naval expeditionary force to attack the common territory of Bushehr. Which was the primary port of entry into Persia at that time. Lord Canning decided to pass this act, which forced deployment abroad. Due to the punishment of 'Kala Pani' (black water), sea travel was opposed. Thus, it was one of the main reasons for the great rebellion of 1857
