questions.question_text: Which of the following was not a part of the 1832-33 Kol revolt?
questions.explanation: Tribals played an important role in the Indian freedom movement. The Kol revolt has a prominent place among tribal revolts. The Kol revolt that started in 1831 AD was eventually suppressed by the British with their power and diplomacy. The Toto tribe was not involved in this. The Toto tribe is found in West Bengal

questions.question_text: Who helped the British in suppressing the Bundela revolt of 1842?
questions.explanation: Participation in the Bundela revolt in Bundelkhand is recorded on 8 April, 1842 AD. Many Bundela, Lodhi, and Gond Thakurs participated, including Madhukar Shah and Ganesh of Narhat, Jawahar Singh of Chandrapur, Vikramjit Singh of Gudha, Bakht Singh of Chirgaon, Bhujabal Singh and Mahipal Singh of Jakhlone and Pipariya, Raja Hirdeshah of Hirapur, Dalen Singh of Madanpur and Gond Thakur of Dilwara, Natwar Singh, etc. Charles Fraser prepared the strategy to suppress the Bundela revolt. Thakur Madan Singh and Raja Bakhtawali, Scindia of Gwalior, the Queen of Orchha, etc., have helped the British to suppress the Bundela revolt. The British asked for help from Shahgarh Raja Bakhtawali and Banpur Raja Madan Singh, because the Bundela rebels were also looting their princely states and these two Rajas wanted to get back their area occupied by Scindia with the help of the British, so both these Rajas were ready to help the British. Shahgarh Raja Bakhtawali caught Hirapur Raja Hirdeshah on 22 December, 1842 AD and handed him over to the British. Banpur Raja Madan Singh caught the main rebel Madhukar Shah on 24 January, 1844 AD and handed him over to the British.

questions.question_text: When did the Santhal revolt start?
questions.explanation: The Santhal was a farming tribe whose constant suppression gave birth to their revolt against the Zamindars. The revolt started in 1855-56 under the leadership of Sidhu Manjhi and Kanhu in opposition to the exploitation done by local Zamindars and moneylenders of Bihar, which was eventually ended by the British later

questions.question_text: Who were the leaders of the Khasi revolt?
questions.explanation: The Khasi tribe lived between the Jaintia hills in the east of Bengal province and the Garo hills in the west. Before the British authority, there were 30 separate powerful states of the Khasis. This revolt started in 1829. Its leader was Tirut Singh. In 1833 AD, Tirut Singh surrendered on the condition of not being given the death penalty and this revolt was suppressed

questions.question_text: The play 'Neel Darpan', which inevitably influences the 'Indigo Revolt' of 1859, was written by whom:
questions.explanation: Neel Darpan is a famous play in the Bengali language whose author is Dinabandhu Mitra. It was written in 1858-59 AD. It became the cause of the Indigo movement that took place in Bengal and also became a pioneer for the development of the Bengali stage. It was played at the National Theatre of Kolkata in the year 1872 AD, which was the first play from a professional point of view

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not matched correctly?
questions.explanation: Ramosi Revolt - Ramosi was a primitive tribe living in the Western Ghats. They were very unhappy with the British administration system and British administration. As a result, in 1822, their chieftain Chittur Singh revolted and looted the territory around Satara. In 1825-26, riots happened again and there was unrest in this region till 1829

questions.question_text: What is the correct chronological order of the following revolts? 1. Bundela revolt of Jabalpur 2. Mysore peasants' revolt 3. Veluthampi revolt 4. Revolt of Poligars of Tamil Nadu
questions.explanation: The chronological order of the following revolts is as follows Names of Revolts Year Other 1. Revolt of Poligars of Tamil Nadu This revolt continued for a long time under the leadership of Veerapandya Kattabomman. 2. Veluthampi Revolt In Kerala, Dewan Veluthampi revolted against the imposition of Lord Wellesley's subsidiary alliance on the King of Travancore, in which Veluthampi died. 3. Mysore peasants' revolt 1830-31 4. Bundela revolt of Jabalpur 1842 AD The Bundelas revolted under the leadership of Hirapur Raja Hirdeshah. Note: No option in the above question is correct.

questions.question_text: The famous Bengali writer Dinabandhu Mitra's play 'Neel Darpan' (1860) describes the atrocities of whom?
questions.explanation: Neel Darpan is a famous Bengali play whose author is Dinabandhu Mitra, which was written in 1858-59. This creation describes the atrocities of Indigo plantation owners. It became the cause of the Indigo movement in Bengal. It also became a pioneer of the development of the Bengali stage

questions.question_text: The inspiration for the play 'Neel Darpan' is________type-
questions.explanation: In 1859-60, peasants in Bengal carried out the Indigo revolt, the immediate situation of which is described in this Neel Darpan play, which was written by Dinabandhu Mitra

questions.question_text: The 'Eka' organization in Awadh was related to-
questions.explanation: The Eka movement was actually a peasant movement. This movement was carried out by the peasants of Awadh in 1921-22 AD, which was centered in the Hardoi, Bahraich, Sultanpur, Barabanki, and Sitapur regions. Its main leaders Madari Pasi and Sahdev both belonged to lower castes. The main reason for this movement was excessive rent and taking away fields illegally

questions.question_text: The founders of the Vidya Pracharini Sabha, prevalent during the Bijolia peasant movement, were:
questions.explanation: Vijay Singh Pathik was the founder of the Vidya Pracharini Sabha (1914 AD) prevalent during the Bijolia peasant movement. Vijay Singh Pathik was also associated with the Rajasthan Seva Sangh (1919 AD) and Madhya Bharat Sabha (1919 AD)

questions.question_text: In which play written by Dinabandhu Mitra has the exploitation of the garden laborers of Bengal been highlighted?
questions.explanation: Dinabandhu Mitra was a contemporary Bengali playwright of Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay. His first play Neel Darpan (Dacca, 1860) is based on the story of the atrocities of the whites on the contemporary rural peasants. When it was published in 1860, there was a sharp reaction in both Bengali society and the rulers. Bengali society welcomed it and the British rulers hated it. Bringing the Dramatic Performances Control Act by the British government in 1876 was also aimed at suppressing the rebellious spirit of plays like Neel Darpan. James Long published the English translation of Neel Darpan. Other plays of Dinabandhu Mitra are - Leelavati, Kamlekamini

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about peasant movements in India is not correct?

options.A: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati formed the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929.
options.B: The Utkal Kisan Sangh was established in 1938 by the Congress Socialists.
options.C: Congress Socialist Party worker N.G. Ranga organized many peasant marches in Andhra in 1933-34 and demanded the abolition of Zamindari.
options.D: In 1935, N.G. Ranga and E.M.S. Namboodiripad tried to expand the peasant movement in the Madras Presidency and formed the South Indian Federation of Peasants and Agricultural Laborers.

questions.explanation: In the above question, option (b) is false, because the Utkal Kisan Sangh was formed by Malati Choudhary in 1935 AD. It is noteworthy that the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha was formed by Swami Sahajanand Saraswati in 1929 AD Unprecedented awareness was also seen among the peasants in the coastal areas of Andhra. In 1933-34, under the leadership of famous peasant leader N.G. Ranga, the peasants took out many marches and demanded the abolition of Zamindari. N.G. Ranga ran an institution named 'Indian Peasant Council' in his village Nidubrolu in Guntur district in 1933 itself. Along with E.M.S. Namboodiripad, he formed the 'South Indian Federation of Peasants and Agricultural Laborers'.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the tribal revolt is not correct?

options.A: The armed revolt (1876-77) of Vasudev Balwant Phadke erupted rapidly due to Lord Lytton's racial discrimination policies.
options.B: The Santhals of Rajmahal hills revolted in 1855 because they were fed up with the misbehavior of revenue officials, and the atrocities of police, Zamindars, and moneylenders.
options.C: The Ahom aristocratic class of Assam revolted in 1828 because the British power did not fulfill the promise of withdrawing after the Burma war.
options.D: The Vagheras of Okha Mandal revolted in 1818-1819 because with the help of the British government, the Gaekwad rulers of Baroda forcibly collected taxes.

questions.explanation: Moved by the miserable condition of the peasants, the tribal revolutionary Vasudev Balwant Phadke considered 'Swaraj' as the only solution for this. He gathered tribes like Koli, Bhil, etc., of Maharashtra and built a revolutionary organization named 'Ramosi'. In the end, this resistance was stopped through land grants, but by then Phadke had already become a victim of British atrocities. There was no role of Lord Lytton's racial policy in this

questions.question_text: Which tribe was not involved in the Kol tribal revolt of 1832-33?
questions.explanation: In the period of the year 1832-33, the tribes named Chuar, Ho, and Munda participated in the Kol tribal revolt against the British.

questions.question_text: Who among the following wrote the play named 'Neel Darpan'?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2004 Explanation – British Indigo producers in Bengal had long compelled the peasants to forcefully cultivate indigo. On the orders of Deputy Magistrate Hem Chandra, the anger of the peasants flared up, so the peasants of Govindpur village of Nadia district revolted under the leadership of Digambar Biswas and Vishnu Biswas and stopped indigo cultivation. Details of the exploitation of peasants are found in Dinabandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan.

questions.question_text: The Pagal Panthi revolt was actually a revolt of whom?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2013 Explanation ─ The Pagal Panthi revolt was actually a revolt of the Garo tribe 1813-31 AD. It was a semi-religious sect. It was run by Karam Shah in North Bengal. The main center of the rebels was the region of the Garo hills. This was a peasant revolt.

questions.question_text: Which of the following revolts was Birsa the leader of?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2013 Explanation ─ Birsa Munda was the leader of the Munda revolt. He declared himself the messenger of God and ordered his followers to worship Singbonga. In 1900 AD, he was arrested where he died in Ranchi jail.

questions.question_text: Where did the Moplah revolt take place?
questions.explanation: Asharam Paddhati Lect. Exam. 2012 Explanation– The Moplah revolt took place in Kerala. In the beginning, this movement was political, later it took a religious form. Here most of the Zamindars were Hindus while the peasants were Muslims. Those Zamindars exploited the peasants a lot, as a result of which the peasants revolted after getting the opportunity.

questions.question_text: Who led the Khasi revolt against the British?
questions.explanation: PGT History, 2003 Explanation– A tribal tribe named Khasi used to live in the hilly region near the borders of North West Assam. In 1829 AD, they revolted. The chief of the Khasi tribe of Nunklow, Tirut Singh, led this revolt. This revolt was suppressed with cruelty. By the end of 1832 AD, Tirut Singh along with other Khasi chiefs surrendered and the revolt of the Khasis ended.

questions.question_text: To which period does the 'Sannyasi Revolt' belong?
questions.explanation: G.I.C. Lect. Exam 2015 Explanation- Due to the establishment of British rule in Bengal and the establishment of a new economic system because of it, Zamindars, peasants, and artisans all were destroyed. In 1770, a severe famine occurred in Bengal. The British put restrictions on people's movement; Sannyasis were very angry due to the restrictions on movement to pilgrimages and they revolted which lasted from 1763 to 1800 AD. This has also been mentioned in 'Anandamath'. Warren Hastings suppressed this.

questions.question_text: Who led the peasant movement in Bihar in the 1930s?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2001 Explanation- In 1936, the 'All India Kisan Congress' was established in Lucknow, whose name was later changed to 'All India Kisan Sabha'. The fighting founder of the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha, Swami Sahajanand Saraswati, was its President and the leader of the peasant movement in Andhra and scholar of agricultural sector problems, N.G. Ranga, was elected General Secretary. Jawaharlal Nehru himself came to the first conference of the Kisan Sabha and welcomed the organization. Other personalities present in this conference were Rammanohar Lohia, Sohan Singh Josh, Indulal Yagnik, Jayaprakash Narayan, Mohanlal Gautam, Kamala Sarkar. It was decided in the conference that a manifesto of the peasants should be brought out and a bulletin should be published regularly under the editorship of Indulal Yagnik.

questions.question_text: Which of the following was a common cause of all tribal revolts?

options.A: The arrival of Christian missionaries in tribal areas
options.B: Ending the distinctiveness of tribes by colonial administration and bringing them into the periphery of colonialism
options.C: Restricting the access of tribes to forest produce by colonial administration
options.D: Complete disintegration of the old agricultural system of tribal communities by colonial administration

questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2002 Explanation- The common cause of all tribal revolts was to end the distinctiveness of tribes by colonial rule and bring them into the periphery of colonialism. When colonial rule, armed with the weapons of corruption and atrocities, intruded into the areas of tribals, it was natural for them to have deep resentment. Usually, tribals kept themselves separate from the rest of the society. But the British Raj pulled them completely inside the colonial circle. The British Raj gave the status of Zamindars to the chiefs of tribal clans and implemented a new revenue system. Pulled the tribals into the whirlpool of colonial economy and exploitation, which became the cause of the revolt.

questions.question_text: Match List-I with List-II and select your correct answer from the code given below the lists- List-I (Revolt) List-I (Region) A. Bhil 1. Sahyadri B. Koli 2. Meghalaya C. Chuar 3. West Bengal D. Khasi 4. Khandesh Code: A B C D
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2004 Explanation- The Bhil revolt started with the British occupation of Khandesh in 1818, which lasted till 1848. In 1825, the Bhil revolt was led by 'Sevaram'. This revolt was crushed by the army. The revolt of the Koli tribe took place in the Sahyadri mountain region. The Chuar revolt took place in 1766 in five districts of West Bengal and Bihar and lasted till 1772. From 1795 to 1816, the Chuar revolt flared up again. The revolt of the Khasi tribe living in the hills of Meghalaya and Assam took place in 1829-32 under the leadership of Tirut Singh and Barmanik.

questions.question_text: Who was the leader of the Faraizi revolt?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2005 Explanation - The Faraizi people were followers of the sect run by Haji Shariatullah, a resident of Faridpur, Bengal. These people advocated for many religious, social, and political radical changes. Shariatullah's son (Muhammad Mohsin) Dadu Miyan (1819-60) planned to drive the British out of Bengal. This sect was also in opposition to the atrocities committed by Zamindars on their tenants. Faraizi riots continued from 1838 to 1857 and in the end, many followers of this sect joined the Wahabi group.

questions.question_text: Indicate the name of the leader of the Indigo revolt that took place in Bengal in 1860 -
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2007 Explanation - The Indigo movement of Bengal took place in Govindpur village of Nadia district. Actually, the main reason for this revolt was the exploitative nature of European plantation owners. Where peasants wanted to grow rice and wheat on their fertile land. European plantation owners forced them to cultivate indigo on their fertile land. Apart from this, they would make the peasants bonded in a way by giving a small amount of money which was called 'Dadni Pratha'. The price of the indigo that the peasants grew was also much less than the prevailing market price. Seeing all these problems, the peasants revolted under the leadership of 'Sisir Kumar Ghosh'. The theme of Dinabandhu Mitra's play 'Neel Darpan' is based on this plight of the peasants.

questions.question_text: The first tribal group to revolt against the British was-
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2008 Explanation– Kol Revolt – 1831-33 Munda Revolt – 1895-1900 Khasi Revolt – 1829-1833 Santhal Revolt – 1855-56

questions.question_text: The first tribal leader to be influenced by Mahatma Gandhi and his ideology was:
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2008 Explanation - Rampa revolt leader Alluri Sitarama Raju was a non-tribal leader who claimed to have astrological and physical healing powers and soon became the hero of folk tales of Andhra Pradesh. He got inspiration from the Non-Cooperation Movement and was an admirer of Gandhi ji, but he considered violence necessary for the protection of tribal interests.

questions.question_text: Match List I and List II and select the correct answer with the help of the codes given below: List-I List-II A. Faqir B. Ramosi (ii) Karam Shah C. Pagalpanthi (iii) Majnu Shah D. Bihar Kisan Sabha (iv) Chittur Singh Code : A B C D (i) Sahajanand Saraswati
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2008 Explanation – 1. Faqir Revolt – Majnu Shah/Chirag Ali Shah - 1776-77 2. Ramosi - Chittur Singh - 1822, 1825-26 3. Pagalpanthi - Karam Shah/Tippu - 1813-33 4. Bihar Kisan Sabha - Sahajanand 1929 Saraswati 'Kisan Pran'

questions.question_text: Find the correct chronological order of the revolts against British rule from the code given below– A. Sannyasi Revolt 1. 1855-56 B. Kol Revolt 2. 1760 C. Santhal Revolt D. Moplah Revolt 4. 1831-32 Code : A B C D 3. 1921
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2010 Explanation– Sannyasi revolt took place in Bengal in 1760, which has been described by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay in 'Anandamath'. Kol revolt continued from 1831 to 1837 AD in Ranchi, Singhbhum, and Hazaribagh. Santhal revolt was centered between Bhagalpur and Rajmahal under the leadership of Sidhu and Kanhu. In 1921 AD, the Moplah peasant movement took place in the Malabar district of Kerala under the leadership of Ali Musliyar, which was against the Zamindars.

questions.question_text: Who was the main leader of the Bijolia movement of Rajputana:
questions.explanation: The Bijolia movement was started by the peasants of Mewar state in 1897 AD. It was led by different people at different times in which the names of Sitaramdas, Vijay Singh Pathik, and Manikyalal Verma are notable. This movement ended in 1941

questions.question_text: Who of the following is associated with the Bundela revolt of 1842?
questions.explanation: Raja Hirdeshah was the main hero of the 1842 Bundelkhand revolt. Parichhat and Madhukar Shah were also associated with this revolt. Although this revolt was suppressed by the government, Hirdeshah played a sacrificial role again in the 1857 revolt, in which his entire family was martyred

questions.question_text: Who was associated with the Kuka movement?
questions.explanation: The Kuka revolt was an armed revolt carried out by the Namdhari Sikhs of Punjab in 1871-72, which was basically done in opposition to the promotion of cow slaughter by the British. Balak Singh and his follower Guru Ram Singh ji led it

questions.question_text: Which of the following (Revolt and Leader) is not matched correctly?
questions.explanation: (1) Munda revolt (Munda) - The tribe living in the south of Ranchi of Chota Nagpur plateau was Munda. This movement started in 1895 AD under the leadership of Birsa Munda (2) Santhal revolt - It was centered from Bhagalpur to Rajmahal. This revolt started in 1855 AD under the leadership of Sidhu and Kanhu. (3) Ahom revolt - Ahom were the aristocratic class living in Assam. In 1828 AD, the Ahoms revolted under the leadership of Gomdhar Kunwar. (4) Tana Bhagat movement - The Tana Bhagat movement started in the year 1914 AD as a form of not paying revenue, not doing forced labor (begar), and not paying taxes under the leadership of Jatra Bhagat.

questions.question_text: Madari Pasi is associated with-
questions.explanation: Madari Pasi is associated with the peasant movement of U.P. In the year 1921-22, Madari Pasi and Sahdev ran the Eka movement in the interest of the peasants of Awadh province. The main center of this movement was in the Hardoi, Bahraich, Barabanki, and Sitapur districts of modern Uttar Pradesh

questions.question_text: (i) Rampa (ii) Santhal (iii) Kol (iv) Munda under the leadership of Birsa Select the correct answer from the code given below: Code: Arrange the following tribal revolts chronologically:
questions.explanation: UGC NET-III Paper Jan. 2017 Explanation– Among the tribal revolts given in the options, the Kol revolt happened first. In 1831 AD, the Kols either burnt or murdered about 1000 foreigners or outsiders. This revolt took place in the western regions of Ranchi, Singhbhum, Hazaribagh, Palamau, and Manbhum. After this, the Santhal revolt happened. This revolt of Santhals took place in Rajmahal district in 1855-56 under the leadership of Sidhu and Kanhu. After this, the Rampa tribal revolt took place in 1879 AD. People of the Munda tribe near Ranchi revolted during 1895-1900. Birsa Munda gave leadership to it.

questions.question_text: Arrange the following peasant revolts that occurred in the second half of the nineteenth century in correct chronological order: (i) Kuka revolt of Punjab (ii) Peasant revolt of Pabna district (iii) Indigo revolt of Bengal (iv) Peasant movement of Deccan Select the correct answer with the help of the code: Code:
questions.explanation: Indigo revolt of Bengal - 1859-60 Kuka revolt of Punjab - 1860-70 Peasant revolt of Pabna district - 1873-76 Peasant movement of Deccan - 1875

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be called the 'first general revolt' of the Indian peasant class?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2004 Explanation– Santhal revolt occurred in 1856 AD in Rajmahal district due to exploitation and misbehavior of British officials, whereas the revolt in Bengal in 1859 under the leadership of Digambar Biswas and Vishnu Biswas is called the 'first general revolt'.

questions.question_text: If the spade was the symbol of Pahariya life in Rajmahal hills, then the symbol of Santhals was ........
questions.explanation: If the spade was the symbol of Pahariya life in Rajmahal hills, then the symbol of Santhals was 'plough'

questions.question_text: Which tribe (tribe) of the nineteenth century is associated with the movement named "Hul"?
questions.explanation: Before the revolt of 1857 AD, the Hul revolution against the British took place in Santhal Parganas. This revolt was mainly carried out by the Santhal tribals. This revolt was carried out to express their resentment against the misbehavior at the hands of land revenue officials, suppression by the police, and collections by Zamindars-moneylenders. Two Santhals named Sidhu and Kanhu provided leadership to the Santhal revolt. However, to suppress the Santhal revolt, the government imposed martial law in the violence-affected areas and announced an award of ten thousand to catch the rebel leaders. Finally, Sidhu and Kanhu were caught and sentenced to death

questions.question_text: Who published a series of articles titled 'New Lamps for Old' in which criticism of moderate politics was presented?
questions.explanation: Aurobindo Ghosh published a series of articles in 1893 A.D. titled 'New Lamps for Old' in which he presented criticism of moderate politics Special Facts Author Newspapers/Books (1) Aurobindo Ghosh (1) Bande Mataram, (2) Karmayogin, (3) Essays on Gita (4) Divine Life (Autobiography) (2) Lala Lajpat Rai (1) Punjabi, (2) Bande Mataram, (3) The People, editing of the magazine (3) Bal Gangadhar Tilak (1) Editing of newspapers like Maratha and Kesari (2) Gita Rahasya (3) The Arctic Home in the Vedas (4) Bipin Chandra Pal (1) My Life and Times (2) Memories of My Life and Times (3) The New India

questions.question_text: Who was given the death penalty for shooting the District Magistrate of Nashik, A. Jackson?
questions.explanation: Anant Laxman Kanhere was given the death penalty for shooting the District Magistrate of Nashik, A. Jackson Special Facts 1. India House member Madan Lal Dhingra shot and killed the political advisor to the Secretary of State for India, William Curzon Wyllie, on July 1, 1909. Soon after, Dhingra was hanged. 2. Damodar Chapekar and Balkrishna Chapekar laid the foundation of revolutionary terrorist activities in India by killing Pune's Plague Commissioner Rand and Ayerst on June 22, 1897. Later, the Chapekar brothers were hanged. 3. Prafulla Chaki and Khudiram Bose attempted to kill the Bengal Presidency Magistrate Kingsford on April 30, 1908. Prafulla Chaki committed suicide to escape the police, and Khudiram Bose was arrested and hanged.

questions.question_text: Who was sent to the cellular jail for life imprisonment?
questions.explanation: Vasudev Balwant Phadke (1845-1883 A.D.) was a revolutionary of the Indian freedom struggle from Maharashtra. He was deeply disturbed by the pathetic condition of farmers in British India. He adopted an armed path to oppose British rule. He organized tribes like Koli, Bhil, etc., in Maharashtra and formed an organization named Ramoshi. They had taken the Pune district under their control for some time. Due to anti-British activities, he was arrested, sentenced to life imprisonment, and put in the Aden jail. He died here

questions.question_text: "We want to be born from the womb of the same mother (Bharat Mata) and want to die for the same purpose again, until our purpose is completely successful." Whose statement is this?
questions.explanation: "We want to be born from the womb of the same mother (Bharat Mata) and want to die for the same purpose again, until our purpose is completely successful" - this statement is by Madan Lal Dhingra. Madan Lal Dhingra (1883-1909 A.D.) was a revolutionary of the Indian freedom struggle who killed Curzon Wyllie in England by shooting him. In 1909, he was tried and sentenced to death. He was the first revolutionary to be hanged abroad

questions.question_text: Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below: List-I List-II (Revolt) (Associated Leader) A. Ramosi Revolt 1. Tirath Singh B. Santhal Revolt 2. Govind Kunwar C. Khasia Revolt 3. Chittur Singh D. Ahom Revolt 4. Sidhu Kanhu A B C D

questions.question_text: When was a weekly magazine named 'Ghadar' first published?
questions.explanation: At the end of the 19th century, many Indians went and settled in America and Canada. On 1 November 1913 A.D., the Ghadar Party was formed in San Francisco city of America. Its founder was Lala Hardayal, while the president of this party was Sohan Singh Bhakna. Other prominent leaders of this group were - Ram Chandra, Barkatullah, Rash Behari Bose, Raja Mahendra Pratap, Abdul Rahman, and Madame Bhikaiji Cama. The Ghadar Party established the Yugantar Press and published a weekly (later monthly) magazine 'Ghadar'

questions.question_text: Famous revolutionary Ashutosh Kuila was a member of which revolutionary organization?
questions.explanation: Famous revolutionary Ashutosh Kuila was a member of the revolutionary organization named Vidyut Bahini. On 17 December, 1942, the Tamralipta National Government was established in Tamluk of Midnapore district of Bengal. The government formed an armed Vidyut Bahini. The national government remained in existence until 1 September, 1944 A.D

questions.question_text: Which of the following was not related to the Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy Case?
questions.explanation: On 17 March, 1924, S.A. Dange, M.N. Roy, Muzaffar Ahmed, Nalini Gupta, Shaukat Usmani, Singaravelu Chettiar, Ghulam Hussain, and others were accused that as communists they were demanding to completely deprive the King Emperor of British India of his sovereignty. 'To separate India from imperialist Britain through a violent revolution'. Which was called the Kanpur Bolshevik Conspiracy case. In this case, people's interest was attracted towards the Comintern plan of bringing a violent revolution in India. Newspaper pages bombarded people with sensational communist plans and people for the first time learned on a large scale about communism, its principles, and the objectives of the Communist International in India

questions.question_text: Which of the following freedom fighters established the "Indian Home Rule Society" in England?
questions.explanation: Shyamji Krishna Varma established the India Home Rule Society in England in 1905. The purpose of establishing this organization was to provide facilities for living and food/drink to Indian scholars and students in England at a low cost, and this facility was also given to them on the condition that after receiving education in England, they would not work for anyone under the British government in India. Detailed information about this was given in the Sedition Committee report

questions.question_text: Which of the following revolutionaries established the "Abhinav Bharat" organization?
questions.explanation: The Abhinav Bharat organization was established by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar. His name was foremost among the revolutionary associations of Maharashtra. This organization was established in 1904 A.D. In 1899 A.D., an organization named Mitra Mela was established, which later became famous as Abhinav Bharat Society. Its branches were active in many areas of Maharashtra and Central Provinces

questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs is not matched?

options.C: Madan Lal Dhingra - Killing of Curzon Wyllie
options.D: Khudiram Bose - Bomb attack on Lord Hardinge

questions.explanation: The bomb on Lord Hardinge was not thrown by Khudiram Bose, but it was thrown by Basant Biswas and Manmath Biswas, two brothers who were servants of Rash Behari Bose. Its main initiator was Rash Behari Bose himself. At that time (1912), the capital of British India was being shifted from Calcutta to New Delhi; Lord Hardinge was the Viceroy. This bomb case is also known as the Delhi Conspiracy. In this, Rash Behari Bose went to Japan to avoid arrest. Khudiram Bose threw a bomb at Kingsford in 1908. Prafulla Chaki also assisted him in this. Due to which Khudiram Bose was hanged and Prafulla Chaki committed suicide. Because in this, Mr. Kennedy and his wife, who had sympathy for Indian independence, were killed, due to which Prafulla Chaki felt remorse India House was established in London by Shyamji Krishna Varma in 1905. Barindra Kumar Ghosh's association is related to the 1905 revolution. He wrote a book named 'Bhawani Mandir'. Madan Lal Dhingra killed Curzon Wyllie (British officer) in London by shooting him. For which Dhingra was tried in July 1909. He was sentenced to death.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs of Indian revolutionaries abroad and their newspapers are not correct?
questions.explanation: Tarak Nath Das was an Indian revolutionary. The newspaper edited by him was Free Hindustan, whereas the newspaper edited by Ramnath Puri was Secular-e-Azadi. The newspaper edited by Shyamji Krishna Varma was Indian Sociologist. The paper written by Indubhushan Deshmukh was 'America Through Indian Eyes', whereas the Gaelic American was an Irish nationalist newspaper published in the United States from 1903 to 1951, which was with the 'Irish nation owned by John Devoy'. It was restarted as an online news publication in 2021

questions.question_text: Who said that "Communalism is as big an enemy as colonialism"?
questions.explanation: "Communalism is as big an enemy as colonialism", this statement is of Bhagat Singh. Indian revolutionary and freedom fighter Bhagat Singh (1907-1931 A.D.) was a great revolutionary of India. He was the founder of 'Naujawan Bharat Sabha' and a member of the 'Hindustan Socialist Republican Association'. Along with Rajguru and Chandra Shekhar Azad, he killed the military officer Saunders, responsible for the death of Lala Lajpat Rai, in Lahore in 1928 A.D. He believed in leftist ideology and was a firm supporter of socialism. He strongly opposed imperialism and colonialism and considered communalism as big an enemy as imperialism. Along with Batukeshwar Dutt, he threw a bomb in the Central Assembly on 8 April, 1929 A.D., and as a result, he was arrested and hanged on 23 March, 1931

questions.question_text: In which Bengali novel is the nationalist song 'Vande Mataram' contained?
questions.explanation: The eternal and immortal national song of India 'Vande Mataram' is taken from the famous revolutionary novel 'Anandamath', which filled the national movement in India during that period with the feeling of patriotism and nationalism. Vande Mataram mantra proved to be such a panacea that in the next 127 years the country awakened from its sleep and transformed into a wide-awake nation. The creator of this novel is `Bankim Chandra Chatterjee'

questions.question_text: In which year was Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel "Anandamath" published?
questions.explanation: Anandamath is also considered the first political novel of modern Indian literature. Soon after publication, Anandamath became closely associated with the mass movement of independence, and one aspect of it, our national song Vande Mataram, is still a subject of political debate. Anandamath was published as a book in 1882 A.D. Before this, it had already been published serially in Bankim Chandra's magazine Bangadarshan

questions.question_text: What was Komagata Maru?
questions.explanation: Komagata Maru was a Japanese ship powered by steam, which was rented by Baba Gurdit Singh who lived in Hong Kong. Baba set off for Vancouver on 4 March 1914 by seating 376 people of Punjab in the ship and reached Vancouver on 23 May, but the administration there sent the ship back

questions.question_text: Which of the following was not an extremist leader?

questions.question_text: Where was the headquarters of the Ghadar party located?
questions.explanation: The Ghadar party was established in San Francisco in November 1913, its headquarters was also here. The purpose of this organization operating from outside India was established to free India from the British. Among its founder members were Lala Hardayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna, Santokh Singh, and Baba Jawala Singh were the prominent leaders

questions.question_text: Who established an 'India Home Rule Society', a revolutionary organization outside India?
questions.explanation: India Home Rule Society was an Indian organization established in London in 1905, which demanded to promote the cause of self-rule in British India. The organization was established by Shyamji Krishna Varma. Madan Lal Dhingra, Lala Hardayal, Ajit Singh, and V.D. Savarkar were its members

questions.question_text: Where was the revolutionary organization 'Abhinav Bharat' established?
questions.explanation: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and Ganesh Savarkar started a revolutionary secret society Mitra Mela in Nashik in 1899. In 1904, in a meeting of 200 members from various towns of Maharashtra, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar named it Abhinav Bharat. Due to Savarkar's revolutionary propaganda, on the evening of 1 July 1909, Madan Lal Dhingra killed Lt. Col. William Curzon Wyllie in a meeting of Indian students. The District Magistrate of Nashik, A.M.T. Jackson, was also finally killed by Laxman Kanhere in the historic Nashik Conspiracy case, after which in 1910 Vinayak Damodar Savarkar was imprisoned in the Cellular jail of Andaman

questions.question_text: Select the revolutionaries who remained active after 1930: 1. Surya Sen, 2. Kalpana Datta, 3. Ram Prasad Bismil, 4. Bhagawati Charan Vohra. Select the correct code.
questions.explanation: Surya Sen (Master da), Anant Singh, Ambika Chakravarty, Kalpana Datta, Lokenath, Pritilata Waddedar, Ganesh Ghosh, Fakir Ahmed Mir, Tanu Miyan, Subodh, etc., were members of the Indian Republican Army (IRA). It was established in 1930 in Chittagong (Bengal) by Surya Sen. Surya Sen was hanged on 12 January 1934 and Kalpana Datta was sentenced to life imprisonment Ram Prasad Bismil was a member of the Hindustan Republican Association HRA (October, 1924, Kanpur), who was hanged (Gorakhpur jail) for the crime of the Kakori conspiracy (9 August 1925 A.D.). Bhagawati Charan Vohra was a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA 10 September, 1928, Ferozeshah Kotla, Delhi). He was the author of 'The Philosophy of the Bomb'.

questions.question_text: Who became the president of the 'Hindi Association of the Pacific Coast of America' in 1913 A.D.?
questions.explanation: The president of the 'Hindi Association of the Pacific Coast of America' formed in America in 1913 A.D. was Sohan Singh Bhakna. Lala Hardayal was among the prominent members of the India Home Rule Society. The main objective of this society was to achieve self-rule for India

questions.question_text: An Englishman named Philip Spratt was sentenced in:
questions.explanation: To stop the growing influence of communists, the British government arrested 33 communists on 20 March 1929 and tried the Meerut Conspiracy Case against them, in which 3 Englishmen - Philip Spratt, Ben Bradley, and Lester Hutchinson were also there. In this case, Muzaffar Ahmed was sentenced to life imprisonment (transportation) and 27 defendants were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. It is noteworthy that in this case, Jawaharlal Nehru, M.A. Ansari, Kailash Nath Katju, and M.C. Chagla appeared on behalf of the defendants

questions.question_text: Who said that `Political freedom is the life breath of a nation'?
questions.explanation: TGT History, 2011 Explanation- Aurobindo Ghosh said that ‘‘Political freedom is the life breath of a nation’’. After being released from the Alipore Conspiracy case, Aurobindo Ghosh gave his political and philosophical thoughts. Later on, he renounced terrorist activities and became an ascetic and established his ashram in Pondicherry.

options.A: He was a resident of Kathiawar
options.B: He started a monthly magazine 'Indian Sociologist'
options.C: He established a hostel in London for Indian students, which was called 'India House'

On the name of the Ghadar magazine only, the 'Hind Association of America' came to be called 'Ghadar Movement'. options.D: Members of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh

questions.question_text: Which school gave the name 'Aryan' to Indian history?
questions.explanation: In the process of enthusiastic discussion of the Vedic period by Orientalists and viewing the lives of ancient Indian people in a pleasant way, the conflict between them was ignored. Orientalists and Indologists prepared a common genealogy of the Indo-European motherland along with the concept of Sanskrit-Greek linguistic similarity and Aryan-Greek people. questions.question_text: Who were given the death sentence in the Delhi Conspiracy Case?

options.A: Avadh Bihari, Amir Chand, Balmukund and Basant Kumar
options.B: Rash Behari Bose, Balraj, Hansraj Sahay
options.C: Rash Behari Bose, Hansraj Sahay, M. Farooqi

questions.explanation: A clear expression of revolutionary activities in Delhi is seen in the Delhi Conspiracy Case. In 1911, an announcement was made to shift the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi. In commemoration of which, programs were organized in Delhi on 23 December, 1912. During the entry in this very program, a bomb attack was made by revolutionaries on Lord Hardinge's procession at a place called Chandni Chowk, in which Rash Behari Bose and Sachindra Nath Sanyal had a major role. After this incident, 13 people were arrested, in which Avadh Bihari, Balmukund, Amir Chand and Basant Kumar were given the death sentence, while Rash Behari Bose succeeded in escaping arrest

questions.question_text: The Hindu Mahasabha was founded on 09 April, 1915 in Haridwar. The speaker of the first presidential address of the Hindu Mahasabha was:
questions.explanation: The Hindu Mahasabha was formed in Haridwar on 9 April, 1915. The speaker of the first presidential address of this conference was Maharaja Manindra Chandra Nandi. Mahatma Gandhi and Swami Shraddhanand were also present at this conference. Later in 1921, the name of this organization was changed to Akhil Bharatiya Hindu Mahasabha. Prominent nationalist leaders associated with this organization were Madan Mohan Malviya, Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, B.S. Moonje, etc

questions.question_text: Who made the 25th and 42nd Amendments?
questions.explanation: The 25th Constitutional Amendment was made in 1971. Through this, Article 31 was amended and it was provided that other articles of the Constitution should not become obstacles in the acquisition of property for public purposes. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment was made in 1976 during the Emergency. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment is called the Mini Constitution. By this amendment, comprehensive amendments were made to the Constitution. Both these constitutional amendments took place during the time of the country's Iron Lady and Prime Minister Smt. Indira Gandhi

questions.question_text: Who was the first Indian Judge in the International Court of Justice?
questions.explanation: B.N. Rau (Benegal Narsing Rau) was born on 26 February 1887 in Mangalore, British India. He is known as the Chief Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India. He had the honor of becoming a permanent judge in the International Court of Justice, which is in The Hague city of the Netherlands, and is the main judicial organ of the United Nations

questions.question_text: At which of the following places was the resolution on Fundamental Rights passed in the 1931 session of the Indian National Congress?
questions.explanation: The resolution on Fundamental Rights was passed in the Karachi session (1931 AD) of the Indian National Congress. The Congress was no longer prepared to limit itself only to Swarajya or the attainment of independence, rather it wanted to present a blueprint of social and economic reforms for Indians so that all people (women and men) could walk with their heads held high, meaning now social and economic objectives were also added along with independence

questions.question_text: In the British Indian Army, who started the maximum number of reforms?
questions.explanation: Kitchener was a British military leader and politician who organized armies on an unprecedented scale as Secretary of State for War during the first years of the First World War. He was also depicted on the most famous British army recruitment poster to date. He participated in the failed operation to rescue General Charles Gordon in Khartoum in 1884-85 and was appointed Governor-General of Eastern Sudan in 1886. In 1900, he was appointed Chief of Staff for British Commander Lord Roberts in the Boer War. For the leadership of this war, he was called 'Creedem of the Boers'. Ultimately, he strengthened the British Indian Army through reforms throughout his life

questions.explanation: 'Star of India', a non-hereditary title of knighthood for both Europeans and Indians, was started to be awarded in 1861. The title of Knighthood or Sir is one of the highest titles of the British government. This title can be given to any person who does good work for society and humanity at the national or international level. So far only two Indians have been awarded the "Knighthood Order of the British Empire" - Rabindranath Tagore (in 1915), Ratan Tata. questions.question_text: Who was the editor of 'Samvad Prabhakar'?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2003 Explanation- At the beginning of the 20th century, Indians also took steps towards the publication of newspapers. In 1816, Gangadhar Bhattacharya brought out a weekly newspaper named 'Bengal Gazette' in English. In 1818 AD, under the supervision of J.C. Marshman, the first newspaper in the local language Bengali 'Digdarshan' was started. But it did not last long. In the same year, a weekly paper started by Marshman, 'Samachar Darpan', continued to be published for a sufficient time. 'Samvad Prabhakar' was edited by Ishwar Chandra Gupta. In 1821, with the encouragement of Raja Rammohan Roy, a weekly paper 'Samvad Kaumudi' was started. Raja Rammohan Roy himself started the publication of 'Mirat-ul-Akhbar' in Persian and 'Brahmanical Magazine' in English. To oppose his views, in 1822 AD, a newspaper named 'Samachar Chandrika' was started by some other people.

questions.question_text: Who is called the 'father of modern Urdu poetry'?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History Spl., 2004 Explanation- The father of modern Urdu poetry is Wali Deccani. Till the 18th century, Urdu was known as 'Rekhta' or 'Deccani'. Sultanate-era scholar Amir Khusrau is called the father of poetry in 'Hindi' or 'Hindustani' language. Khusrau, who was born in Patiyali (Kasganj, Uttar Pradesh), is considered the inventor of Qawwali singing and a new musical instrument 'Sitar'. Mirza Ghalib is a modern Urdu poet and litterateur.

questions.explanation: The Royal Indian Navy mutiny of 18 February, 1946 started in Bombay, when 1100 sailors of H.M.I.S. Talwar revolted due to reasons of discrimination. questions.question_text: After hesitation for several years, in which of the following years did the Indian National Congress officially accept the theory of Drain of Wealth and declared that famine and mass poverty in India were brought about by the drain of wealth?
questions.explanation: In the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress, Dadabhai Naoroji's theory of Drain of Wealth was accepted for the first time. First of all, Dadabhai Naoroji highlighted the theory of drain of wealth in his book 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1867 AD) and declared that the cause of famine and mass poverty in India is the drain of wealth. Nationalist leader Ramesh Chandra Dutt emphasized the theory of drain of wealth in his book 'Economic History of India'

questions.question_text: Who presented a research paper 'England's Debt to India' in May 1867 and was the first acknowledged theorist of drain of wealth?
questions.explanation: During the British era, the theory of drain of wealth (Drain Theory) was presented by Dadabhai Naoroji in 1867 AD through a research paper "England's Debt to India". The exploitative economic policy of colonial rule was strongly opposed by the nationalist thinkers of that time, among whom were mainly Dadabhai Naoroji (Grand Old Man of India), M.G. Ranade, Ramesh Chandra Dutt, G.V. Joshi, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, etc. They assessed that British colonialism, by increasing commercialism, with G.V. Joshi, G.K. Gokhale, G. Subramania Iyer, Prithvi Chandra Ray and many other leaders, raised fundamental questions about the nature and purpose of British rule. According to them, the core element of British imperialism lay in bringing the Indian economy under the British economy. They were successful in seeing that colonialism was no longer being operated through the crude methods of loot, nazrana (gifts) and mercantilism, but through the deceitful and complex mechanism of free trade and foreign capital investment, by turning India into a supplier of food items and raw materials for the British metropolis, and by turning India into a market for metropolitan manufacturers. From the 1840s onwards, British economists and officials saw foreign capital investment along with the legal system as a key instrument for India's development, which was strongly rejected by the early Indian nationalists. They argued that foreign capital, instead of encouraging and increasing Indian capital, replaced and suppressed it, due to which capital flowed out of India and British control over the Indian economy became stronger. They also shed light on the slow decay and destruction of India's traditional crafts in the interest of British manufacturers. The political consequences of such policies were also no less harmful and these became the cause of India's political subjugation. turned India into a consumer of manufactured goods, which led to a decline in the development of traditional Indian handicrafts industry and indigenous goods. From the 1840s onwards, British economists placed more emphasis on the investment of foreign capital rather than Indian capital, which was strongly opposed by the nationalists. The nationalists had become aware that British economic policy is to make India hollow. Therefore, they unitedly rejected the theory of drain of wealth.

questions.question_text: Which of the following Indian nationalists opposed the free trade policy of British rule:
questions.explanation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang (1850-1893) was a judge and linguist of India. Inspired by the nationalist movement, he contributed to the public movements and mass awakening of Bombay in the latter half of the 19th century. He strongly opposed the free trade policy of British rule, British protectionism, and the government's famine policy. He found that colonialism was turning India into a market through the policy of loot, nazrana and mercantilism, and free trade. He accused the British that the policy of free trade is destroying India's handicraft industry and the objective of government expenditure is to fulfill colonial interests, not to develop and welfare of India

questions.question_text: Who said that railways and telegraphs were less beneficial for India and they were like "decorating someone else's wife"?
questions.explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak described the development of railways and telegraphs as disadvantageous for India. In this context, he argued that it is exactly the same as feeling happy after seeing the decoration of someone else's wife. He said that the British did the development of railways and telegraphs for the purpose of fulfilling commercial interests, not for the progress of India. Through railways, agricultural products and raw materials were exported rapidly, as a result, India's cottage industry, handloom industry, jute industry, etc., declined rapidly and India became flooded with British manufactured goods market and became an importer of manufactured goods even against its will

questions.question_text: Which of the following British economists/administrators argued that British economic policies were responsible for bringing economic stability in India? Select the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation: John Stuart Mill and Alfred Marshall argued that British economic policy was mainly responsible for bringing economic stability in India. In the 19th century, British economists and officials considered foreign capital investment along with the legal system as a key for India's development Stuart Mill (1806-1873) was an economist, philosopher, historian. He was a supporter of colonialism and capitalism and a follower of British economic policy. "Principles of Political Economy" (1848) is his major book. Alfred Marshall (1842-1924) explained economics on the theory of demand and supply, his major book is "Principles of Economics" (1890). He was a supporter of British economic policy in the context of India.

questions.question_text: The map of Hindustan made by Major James Rennell in 1783 was indicative of what?

options.A: Attempt to establish Western cartography in the Indian subcontinent
options.B: Import of American method of map making

questions.explanation: Major James Rennell (1742-1830) was a British geographer. He joined the East India Company while serving in the Royal Navy. James Rennell is also called the father of oceanography. He was also a founding member of the 'Royal Geographical Society' in London in 1830. Rennell's first and influential work was Bengal Atlas (1779). After that, in 1783, he made a detailed map of India, which used the European scientific method of map making along with the support of the Indian method. In which perambulator, calibrated wheel and compass were prominent. His other important works include- Geographical System of Herodotus (1800) and Comparative Geography of Western Asia (1831). He published a book named 'Memoir of a Map of Hindoostan' (1788) and dedicated it to Sir Joseph Banks

questions.question_text: After surveying the land in Bombay Presidency, how much percentage of the net value of produce did R.K. Pringle set as the state's land revenue demand?
questions.explanation: After surveying the land in Bombay Presidency, R.K. Pringle set the state's land revenue demand at 55 percent of the net value of the produce Special Facts The Ryotwari system in the Bombay Presidency started under the supervision of Mountstuart Elphinstone, a disciple of Captain Munro. In these areas, the British continued to collect revenue with the help of Deshmukhs and village heads or Patels. The British did not get revenue according to expectations from such collection. Due to this, later they started collecting revenue directly from the farmers, this type of misbehavior became a feature of the Bombay Presidency, because the fixed rates of revenue were high to an extraordinary limit. Repeatedly crops getting destroyed and prices falling forced farmers to either mortgage land to moneylenders or leave farming and go to neighboring princely states where rates were low. Therefore, an officer named R.K. Pringle conducted a land survey; he classified the land and set the revenue rate at 55 percent of the net value of the produce.

questions.question_text: Name those I.N.A. soldiers whose case was heard in the Red Fort of Delhi:
questions.explanation: The British government filed cases against the arrested soldiers and officers of the Azad Hind Fauj in the Red Fort of Delhi in November 1945 AD. The main accused of this case were three officers Major General Shah Nawaz Khan, Colonel Prem Sahgal and Colonel Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon, who were charged with treason. As their defense side, the Congress formed the 'Azad Hind Fauj Bachao Samiti', in which prominent lawyers were Tej Bahadur Sapru, Kailash Nath Katju, Aruna Asaf Ali and Jawaharlal Nehru under the leadership of Bhulabhai Desai. questions.question_text: 'Deliverance Day' was celebrated by the Muslim League in:
questions.explanation: In 1939 AD, on the outbreak of the Second World War, the then Viceroy Lord Linlithgow involved India in the war without the consent of the Indian legislative assemblies. Along with this, a state of emergency was announced in the country. The Congress Working Committee demanded the declaration of war objectives and also demanded that after the war India should be made independent. The government ignored this demand. The Viceroy called colonial Swaraj a hollow dialogue. On 23 October, 1939 AD, the Congress Working Committee passed a resolution expressing resentment against the attitude of the British government and asking the Congress ministries to resign. On the order of the Congress Working Committee, Congress ministries resigned in the provinces on 29-30 October, 1939 AD. After the Congress ministries resigned, the Muslim League celebrated 22 December, 1939 AD as Deliverance Day and Thanksgiving Day. In this, Dr. Ambedkar also supported them

questions.question_text: According to Dadabhai Naoroji, what was the per capita income of an Indian in 1867-68 approximately?

According to famous expert on national income, Colin Clark, during 1925-34, the lowest per capita income in the world was of India and China. An Englishman's income was five times more than an Indian's income

questions.question_text: To improve what did Thomas Robertson suggest for 'Route and Branch Reforms'?
questions.explanation: In 1901, Thomas Robertson was appointed as a Special Commissioner to investigate the management of railways. He told that the system of railways in India was the best in the world except for European countries. In the view of Robertson, although the development of railways in terms of area was not enough. Nevertheless, in comparison to Japan, one mile long railway line in India served more people. Regarding the previous return system, T. Robertson wrote in his report- 'Those railway companies which did not see hope of earning extra profit had no incentive for economy. Those railway companies which did more business in the first half of the year and not in the second half got incentive to spend more and more in the relatively bad half of the year because relatively less expenditure in the good half of the year increased their profit whereas in the bad half of the year change expenditure did not affect the guaranteed-minimum profit by the government.'

questions.question_text: When was the U.P. Kisan Sabha formed?
questions.explanation: In the year 1918, Gauri Shankar Mishra, Indranarayan Dwivedi and Malviya ji formed the Uttar Pradesh Kisan Sabha. questions.question_text: Who is the main creator of the much-discussed 'Black Hole' incident?
questions.explanation: The incident of the Black Hole is a story probably made by British officer J.Z. Holwell to gain fame and to boost violent action against the British. In this, Holwell told that the Nawab locked 146 British prisoners in an 18 feet long and 14 feet 10 inches wide room on the night of 20 June, 1756 AD. The next day, only 23 people including Holwell survived. This incident is famous in history by the name of Black Hole. This incident seems false because it is not possible to lock so many people in such a small room. questions.question_text: Due to hunger strike in jail, which freedom fighter died?
questions.explanation: Jatin Das was born in 1904 AD in Bengal. He was a journalist and a revolutionary of the young freedom struggle who contributed significantly to the country for independence. In the year 1925 AD, he was sentenced to jail in the Dakshineswar bomb case and Kakori conspiracy case in which he went on a hunger strike seeing the discrimination happening to prisoners. questions.question_text: Who signed the Treaty of Poona on 13 June, 1817?
questions.explanation: The last phase of the Third Anglo-Maratha War started on the arrival of Hastings. He made an effort to establish British supremacy in India. The Poona British Resident Elphinstone forced Peshwa Baji Rao II to be compelled to abandon the dominance of the Marathas. Compelled, to free himself from the British, the Peshwa started a war against the British. Marathas set fire to the British Residency in Poona and attacked the British camp at a place called Kirkee, but the Peshwa was defeated by the British and surrendered. questions.question_text: In what context was it said that 'The concept of Indian labour class did not exist until the roots of the perception of Indian people started'?

options.C: Indian labour class during the national movement

There was already discontent regarding salary, food, and caste discrimination, these things incited them for the revolt. Regarding this matter, there was a strike. Soon this strike spread to Madras, Karachi and Calcutta as well. On 19 February, 1946, there was a strike in the entire Navy. Twenty thousand naval soldiers, 20 large ships, nearly 100 small ships were involved in this strike. In these ships, either the tricolor was hoisted or the green and red flag started being hoisted. questions.question_text: Who wrote "The Economic History of India"?

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the fundamental elements to activate, maintain, nourish, and preserve the life principle?

When the dungeon was opened on 21 June 1756, only 23 people were found alive, among whom Holwell was also one. He was the one who felt this incident. (ii) Clive's first tenure in Calcutta lasted till 1757-60. In February 1760, he went back to England after handing over the responsibility of Governor to Holwell for a few months. (iii) 22/23 October 1764 - The Battle of Buxar was fought between Hector Munro on one side (British) and the Mughal Emperor (Shah Alam II), the Nawab of Bengal (Mir Qasim), and the Nawab of Awadh (Shuja-ud-Daulah) on the other side. In which the Mughal Emperor was defeated. With this war, the stay of the British in India was confirmed. (iv) 5 February 1765 - Mir Jafar died. He was called 'Robert Clive's jackal'. In the beginning, Mir Jafar was the army chief of Siraj-ud-Daulah. He kept dreaming of becoming the Nawab of Bengal day and night. He remained the Nawab of Bengal from 1756-1775. (v) 12 August 1765 - The Treaty of Allahabad was signed between Robert Clive and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. Through this treaty, the East India Company got permission to interfere in the political and constitutional system of India, due to which the British hold on India became stronger.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is not correct?

options.A: Colonial sources showed the 1857 rebellion as a 'mutiny of the army'.
options.B: Syed Ahmed Khan has shown the loyalty of Muslims towards British power in the 1857 rebellion.
options.C: British 'free traders' supported the monopoly of the East India Company in India and criticized the kings of native states who rebelled against the company.
options.D: R.C. Majumdar refuses to consider the 1857 rebellion as the 'first war of independence'.

questions.explanation: In September 1599 AD, some merchants held a meeting in London under the chairmanship of Lord Mayor. These merchants formed a company in 1599 with the intention of trading with eastern countries, which was named "Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies". England's 'Queen Elizabeth I' granted it a monopoly to trade with eastern countries for 15 years through an order on 31 December 1600 AD. British 'free traders' and the ruling party were not in favor of the company's commercial monopoly. Free traders used to trade by establishing coordination with the kings of native states who rebelled against the company Syed Ahmed Khan was born on 17 October 1817 in Delhi in the 'Sadat yani Syed' family. At the time of the 1857 revolution, he was working for the East India Company. He established modern madrasas in Moradabad in 1858. The Scientific Society was established by him. This is the reason why Syed Ahmed Khan has shown the loyalty of Muslims towards British power in the 1857 rebellion. According to R.C. Majumdar, we can call the 1857 civil rebellion a war of independence, if we consider its meaning as a small struggle against the British, but in that situation, the struggle of the Pindaris against the British or the struggle of the Wahhabis against the Sikhs would also have to be accepted as such. For this reason, R.C. Majumdar refuses to consider the 1857 rebellion as the 'first war of independence'.

Indigo farming stopped. Editor of Hindu Patriot, Harish Chandra Mukherjee played an important role. Deenbandhu Mitra revealed the oppression of indigo plantation owners in his book 'Neel Darpan'. Pabna rebellion (1873-1876) was done by the tenants of Pabna district. Its leaders were Ishaan Chandra Roy, Shambhu Pal. Bankim Chandra and R.C. Dutt were also involved. Ulgulan rebellion (1899-1900) took place in Chhota Nagpur (Jharkhand) under the leadership of Birsa Munda. This rebellion started due to the change in the traditional land system of the Munda tribe, Khuntkatti, or the landlord system of Mundari.

questions.question_text: After the defeat in the Battle of Plassey, Siraj-ud-Daulah fled from the battlefield. Which vehicle did he use?
questions.explanation: UPPCS (Pre) Indian History, 2010 Explanation – Battle of Plassey - The battle took place on 23 June, 1757, between the British East India Company and the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-ud-Daulah, on the banks of the Bhagirathi River in the Nadia district of West Bengal, at a place called Plassey. The British army was led by Robert Clive, while the responsibility of leading the Nawab's army was with Mir Jafar, Mir Madan, and Rai Durlabh. But the Nawab's army commanders, Mir Jafar and Rai Durlabh, betrayed Siraj-ud-Daulah and did not arrive with their military units with full capacity on the battlefield. During the battle, seeing his defeat near, and seeing other soldiers fleeing, Siraj-ud-Daulah himself fled riding a camel.

options.B: Introduction of Honours courses for students.

questions.question_text: The McMahon line was the result of which treaty?
questions.explanation: The McMahon Line is the boundary between India and Tibet. It came into existence as a result of the Simla Agreement in the year 1914. The length of the McMahon line is 890 km

questions.question_text: The immediate cause of the Second Anglo-Mysore War was:
questions.explanation: The immediate cause of the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-1784 AD) was the seizure by the British of a French settlement named Mahe, which was situated in the Mysore state. Hyder Ali asked the British to vacate Mahe, but they refused. Besides this, the violation of the Madras Treaty (1769 AD) by the British and the formation of a Triple Alliance (Hyder Ali, Nizam of Hyderabad and Marathas) by Hyder Ali in 1779 AD were also among the main causes of the Second Anglo-Mysore War

questions.question_text: Two statements are given below, one is called Assertion (A) and the other is called Reason (R): Assertion (A): India's gradual industrialization not only brought capitalists to the forefront of public life but also created an industrial labor class. Reason (R): Contrary to the European situation, in India, there was no open recruitment of laborers from among the ruined farmers; this recruitment generally happened from among the unemployed. Which of the following is correct in the context of the above two statements?

options.A: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.B: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.explanation: Statement (A) and Reason (R) both are correct, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A). Before the 19th century, Indian farmers used to cultivate for livelihood. But the industrial revolution of England in 1813 AD affected local artisans along with Indian capitalists. People who previously cultivated in India now either became laborers in industries or had to farm according to the administration. In this way, the industrial revolution gave birth to a labor class in India which was different from European laborers. Farmers who were earlier owners of their fields now became laborers

questions.question_text: Who introduced the concept of films in India among these?

questions.question_text: In which of the following fields, in the 19th century, does organized state initiative appear?

In 1896, the Indian Medical Service was established. In this way, organized state initiative appears in these fields in the 19th century

questions.question_text: Regarding the promotion of science in colonial India, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation: The rule of the British in India is called the colonial period. This period is considered from 1760 to 1947 AD. To run the British administration smoothly and to fulfill its economic and military interests, the need for technical education was felt. In the 19th century, Indian scientific education became Europe-centered, centripetal and dominating. Moving forward, colonial science became intricately woven into the fabric of colonialism

questions.question_text: Regarding modern music, which of the following statements is not correct?

options.A: In the 19th century, with the decline in royal patronage, the rise of a new urban Western-educated class, which tried to take classical music out of the courts and temples and make it secular, was indicative of a new cultural environment.
options.B: The new cultural environment made fundamental changes in the structure and form of classical music.
options.C: The rise of the nation as a community appropriately defined, reorganized, fostered and consumed Indian classical music.
options.D: The newly developed taste in music, its practice and presentation were entirely inspired by nationalist ideals.

questions.explanation: The word music includes these three arts of singing, playing instruments and dance. Music cannot be separated from the development of the history of civilization and culture. In the 19th century, along with the decline in royal patronage, the rise of a new urban Western-educated class made classical music indicative of a new cultural environment by taking it out of the courts and temples. This new cultural environment made major changes in the structure and forms of music. Moving forward, in the modern music era, it was redefined, reorganized and fostered in a new way. The contribution of social, political and nationalist ideals was considered in developing music

questions.question_text: Regarding the influence of Western ideas on India, which of the following statements is correct?

options.B: The acceptance of Western ideas through English education was equivalent to the acceptance of British rule.

questions.explanation: Along with becoming a political power in India, it became necessary that they needed people of this type who could take their principles forward. In the beginning, English education overwhelmed the upper class through Western ideas. These influences are blossomed in the Brahmo Samaj, Asiatic Society, etc. With the development of the spirit of rationalism, challenges were received regarding the evils and tyranny in Indian cultural traditions, and this also hurt dogmatism. Despite this, it would not be logical to say that the acceptance of Western ideas through English education was equivalent to the acceptance of British rule, because any power depends on dogmatism itself and this education opposed it. This education first gave birth to consciousness and resistance regarding religious ideas and social evils, not regarding political consciousness

questions.question_text: Which of the following principles was not under the Panchsheel Treaty?

options.A: Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty
options.C: Mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs

questions.explanation: The basic basis of Nehru's foreign policy was the "Panchsheel principle". This principle of Panchsheel or the principle of peaceful co-existence was formally established in the India-China treaty of 29 April 1954 AD regarding trade and mutual relations between India and Tibet. This Panchsheel agreement is based on the following five principles (1) Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty. (2) Assurance of mutual non-aggression. (3) Non-interference in each other's internal affairs. (4) Equality and mutual benefit. (5) Peaceful co-existence.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrectly attributed to the author?

options.D: "The final battle will begin soon. Its result will be decisive. We have participated in this struggle and we are proud to do so." -Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru.

After the end of the Non-Cooperation Movement, he announced the adoption of a policy of non-cooperation with the British power by entering the legislative assemblies, for which he formed the Swaraj Party in 1923. He became its first president "The struggle started in 1920 is a struggle of life and death, even if it ends in a month, a year or many years" - M.K. Gandhi has said.

questions.question_text: Regarding James Mill and his Utilitarianism, which of the following statements is not correct?
